reveal.text: A pool works only if every finished object gives its slot back. Here nothing returns a slot, so after four shots the pool is empty for good.

lead.text: Memory can also be saved by not copying what is the same. A forest of 10,000 trees might use one tree mesh of 20,000 bytes. If each tree object carries its own copy of the mesh together with its 12 bytes of position, the forest takes 10,000 × (20,000 + 12) = 200,120,000 bytes, about 200 megabytes, almost all of it the same mesh stored again and again.

afterFigure.text: The **flyweight pattern** keeps one copy of the shared data and has every tree refer to it. The forest then costs 20,000 + 10,000 × 12 = 140,000 bytes, which is about 1,430 times less. The shared data is called the **intrinsic state**, because it belongs to the kind of tree and is the same for every one. What differs between trees, such as the position, is **extrinsic state**, and each instance keeps its own.

diagram.alt: Two ways of storing trees. In the first every tree holds its own 20,000-byte mesh and 12 bytes of position, totalling 200,120,000 bytes for 10,000 trees. In the second all trees point to one shared mesh and keep only their position, totalling 140,000 bytes.
diagram.caption: Sharing the data that never changes. Use the buttons to compare the two.

reveal.text: The mesh is paid for once, and each extra tree costs only its own 12 bytes.

steps.headline: A field has 5,000 rocks. The shared rock mesh is 8,000 bytes, and each rock keeps 16 bytes of position and rotation. Find the memory with and without sharing.

workedSteps.text: Without sharing, each rock carries the mesh and its own 16 bytes, so every rock costs 8,016 bytes.
With sharing the mesh is stored once, and each rock keeps only its own 16 bytes.
The shared total is 8,000 + 80,000 = 88,000 bytes, which saves 40,080,000 − 88,000 = 39,992,000 bytes.

steps.headline: A game has 2,000 enemies that share one 50,000-byte sprite, and each enemy keeps 20 bytes of its own state.

workedSteps.text: The sprite is intrinsic state, stored once, and the 20 bytes are extrinsic state, stored for each enemy.
Sharing stores the sprite once and the state once for each of the 2,000 enemies.

lead.text: A piece of data may be shared only if every instance would have held the same value and no instance ever changes it. A tree's mesh passes, while its position and its current wind sway fail, and if the sway were put inside the shared mesh, every tree would sway in step. **Per-instance state stays outside the flyweight.**

afterFigure.text: A pool reserves its memory before it is needed, and a flyweight adds a level of indirection, so both are worth their cost only when many objects are created and destroyed in play, or when many objects share large data.

reveal.text: Each of the others is different for every enemy, so sharing it would make the enemies identical in that respect.
Sway differs from tree to tree, so it is extrinsic state. Putting it in the shared part would make every tree move together.

lessons.orientation: Trace an object pool and compute the memory a flyweight saves.
lessons.nextAction: Use a uniform grid to cut collision checks and compute cell indices and pair counts.

blocks.text: A game can be unable to create an object even though the total amount of free memory is more than enough, because the free memory is scattered in gaps and none of them is large enough. The gaps appear when a game creates and frees small objects in no particular order, as a shooter does with every bullet it fires and every bullet that lands, and each request for memory also costs a little time.

A pool avoids the requests altogether by creating a fixed set of objects once and reusing them, and a flyweight attacks a different cost, the memory taken by many objects that each hold a copy of the same data, by keeping a single copy that they all share.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to trace a pool of slots through fire and expire events, and compute the memory a shared flyweight saves.
intro.whyItMatters: Memory is limited and slow to request on many devices, so a game that churns through objects needs a plan for reusing them.

recap.keyIdea: A pool reuses a fixed set of objects to avoid allocation and fragmentation, and a flyweight stores data that is identical for every instance once and keeps only the differences with each instance.

blocks.text: The pool trades memory reserved in advance for the absence of allocation and gaps, and it needs a rule for when it is full. The flyweight trades a little indirection for a large saving, provided that only intrinsic data is shared and every instance keeps its own extrinsic data.

recap.nextHook: The last lesson counts the collision checks a world needs, and shows how a grid cuts them by testing only objects that are close together.

lessons.title: Spatial partitioning

reveal.text: Most pairs in a large world are far apart and cannot touch. The next screen counts how many such tests a crowd needs.

lead.text: The simplest way to find which entities collide is to test every pair. Each of n entities pairs with n − 1 others, which makes n × (n − 1) pairings, but each pair appears twice in that count, once from each end, so the number of distinct tests is n(n − 1) ÷ 2. With 4 entities that is 6 tests, with 5 it is 10, and with 6 it is 15.

afterFigure.text: A thousand entities need 1000 × 999 ÷ 2 = 499,500 tests every frame, nearly 30 million tests a second at 60 frames per second. Since **the count grows with the square of the number of entities**, doubling the crowd makes the work about four times as large.

diagram.alt: Entities drawn as dots with a line for every pair. Four entities have 6 pairs, five have 10 and six have 15.
diagram.caption: Every pair of entities is one collision test. Use the buttons to add entities and count the lines.

reveal.text: Doubling the crowd roughly quadruples the work, which is why testing every pair stops being an option as levels fill up.

lead.text: Spatial partitioning keeps entities sorted by where they are, so that only nearby ones are compared. The simplest form is a **uniform grid**. The world is divided into equal square cells, and an entity is stored in the cell that holds its position. The cell is found by dividing each coordinate by the cell size and rounding down: cell column = floor(x ÷ cell size), and cell row = floor(y ÷ cell size). The result is called the **cell index**.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows a world of 1,000 by 1,000 units with 100-unit cells, so it has 10 × 10 = 100 cells. The entity at (250, 730) has column floor(2.5) = 2 and row floor(7.3) = 7, so it sits in cell (2, 7), with rows counted from the top. Entities are stored per cell, so a test needs only the entities of a few cells instead of the whole world. A position exactly on a boundary, such as x = 300, belongs to the cell that starts there.

reveal.text: Rounding down is part of the rule, and for negative x it matters: -0.3 rounds down to -1 and not to 0.

steps.headline: Find the cell of an entity at (480, 90) in a grid of 100-unit cells.

workedSteps.text: The column comes from dividing x by the cell size.
The quotient has a fractional part, and it is rounded down to give the column index.
The row comes the same way from y, so the entity is in cell column 4, row 0.

steps.headline: Find the cell of an entity at (730, 250) in a grid of 50-unit cells.

workedSteps.text: The row comes from y: 250 ÷ 50 is exactly 5, so the row is 5.
The column comes from x in the same way.

lead.text: An entity near the edge of its cell can overlap an entity in the next one, so a collision check looks at the entity's own cell and the eight cells around it, which is 9 cells in all. Moving entities are handled by recomputing the cell index each frame.

afterFigure.text: A cell size close to the largest entity works well. A uniform grid also assumes the entities are spread evenly, and when they crowd into one region, a **quadtree** splits any square holding too many entities into four smaller squares, again and again, and leaves empty areas whole. A BSP tree divides the world with planes in a similar hierarchical way.

diagram.alt: A square world with thirteen entities, most of them crowded in the top left corner. In the first view an even grid divides it. In the second, a quadtree splits the crowded top-left region into smaller and smaller squares and leaves the empty regions whole.

reveal.text: An entity near a cell's edge can overlap one in the next cell, which is why the check looks at the entity's own cell and its eight neighbours.
A cell size close to the entities' size is a better compromise than either extreme.
The saving comes from skipping every pair that is far apart, and it grows as the world gets larger while the cells stay the same size.

lessons.orientation: Count the collision checks a world needs and use a uniform grid to cut them.
lessons.nextAction: You can now describe a game's design with MDA and core loops, tune its numbers, trace a fixed-timestep loop, and choose and trace the patterns that structure it.

blocks.text: Every frame a game must decide which of its entities touch, and the obvious method, which is to test each one against every other, needs 499,500 tests for a thousand entities, repeated sixty times a second. Most of those tests compare things on opposite sides of the world, and no amount of faster code makes the count grow any more slowly as the crowd gets larger.

Spatial partitioning avoids the pointless tests by keeping entities sorted by where they are, so that each entity is compared only with those nearby. A grid of equal cells is the simplest way to do it, and a tree that splits crowded areas into smaller squares handles worlds where the entities bunch together.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to count pairwise tests, compute the cell an entity falls in, and say what a grid and a quadtree each save.
intro.whyItMatters: Collision and nearest-neighbour queries are among the heaviest work in a game, and partitioning is the standard way to keep them affordable.

recap.keyIdea: Testing every pair takes n(n − 1) ÷ 2 checks, a uniform grid files each entity under floor(position ÷ cell size) in each axis so that only its own and neighbouring cells need checking, and a quadtree does the same for crowds that are uneven.

blocks.text: The all-pairs count grows with the square of the number of entities, so a game keeps entities sorted by position. A uniform grid is the simplest sorting, with its cell found by division and rounding down, and a quadtree refines the same idea where entities crowd together.

questions.prompt: In Tetris a row clears only when all ten squares in it are filled. A player leaves one empty square under a block while the rest of the stack stays flat. What is the likeliest effect on how they play next?
hints: Ask what has to happen before a row with a hole in it can clear.
Think about what a player who has seen this once will try to avoid doing next time.
questions.onCorrect: A rule about complete rows says nothing about flat stacks, yet players find that flat stacks are the safe way to play. The next screen names behaviour of this kind.

acceptedIdeas: The hole stays covered until the rows above it clear, so they work to keep the stack flat
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The hole stays covered until the rows above it clear, so they work to keep the stack flat

choices.label: The game fills the hole in after a few seconds, so their play carries on exactly as before
The hole stays covered until the rows above it clear, so they work to keep the stack flat
The rules never mention holes or flat stacks, so play stays the same with or without one

misconceptions.feedback: No rule fills holes. Only a complete row clears, so the hole stays until the rows above it have gone.
The rules never mention them and play still changes. Behaviour that appears once the rules are played is what the lesson calls dynamics.

questions.prompt: A Tetris player lays every S-shaped piece flat against the bottom of the pile rather than standing it on end, to avoid leaving a hole. In MDA, which layer does this behaviour belong to?
hints: Does any rule of the game say which way an S-shaped piece should lie?
Is the way the piece is laid something the game does, something the player does, or something the player feels?
questions.onCorrect: No rule asks for it. Players adopt the habit because a buried hole cannot be cleared until the rows above it have gone.

acceptedIdeas: A dynamic
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A dynamic

misconceptions.feedback: A mechanic is a rule or a piece of data that a program could check, and no rule of Tetris says which way a piece should lie. The habit appears only when people play.
An aesthetic is a feeling the player has, such as challenge. Laying a piece flat is something the player does, and any feeling it produces is a separate matter.

choices.label: A mechanic
A dynamic
An aesthetic

questions.prompt: In a racing game, which of these statements describes an aesthetic?
hints: An aesthetic is something the player feels.
Rules and measurements are written by the designer.
questions.onCorrect: The thrill is an emotional response. The grip limit and track length are rules and data, and early braking is behaviour.

acceptedIdeas: The thrill of staying just ahead of a rival.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The thrill of staying just ahead of a rival.

choices.label: Players brake early before bends to protect their lead.
The thrill of staying just ahead of a rival.
The car loses grip above 120 km/h.
The track is 4 km long.

misconceptions.feedback: A grip limit is a rule with a number in it, so it is a mechanic.
Early braking is behaviour that emerges from the rules, so it is a dynamic.
The length of the track is data that a program holds, so it belongs with the mechanics.

questions.prompt: In the match-three loop the matched tiles vanish with a sound and a flash. What job does that step do for the player?
hints: Picture the same swap with no flash, no sound and no change on screen.
The player has to decide what to do next. What would they need to know first?
questions.onCorrect: Feedback is how the player learns what an action did, and the next action depends on it.

acceptedIdeas: It shows what the swap did, so the player can choose the next swap
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It shows what the swap did, so the player can choose the next swap

choices.label: It adds the points, which is the reward that sends the player round again
It tells the player the level is over, which ends the loop
It shows what the swap did, so the player can choose the next swap

misconceptions.feedback: The points and the falling tiles are the reward step. The flash and sound are the feedback step, which shows the player what their action just did.
The loop does not end here. The feedback step leads on to the reward and then to the next swap, so the cycle returns to its start.

questions.prompt: A team's platformer has a jump that feels stiff and coins that give little back. Playtesters stop after ten minutes. The team plans to add twenty levels, a world map and a shop. What does the idea of a core loop suggest?
hints: Which cycle does the player repeat most often, ten minutes in or an hour in?
Think about what a new level, a map or a shop sends the player back into.
questions.onCorrect: Outer loops and new levels multiply whatever the core loop is like. A loop that is not satisfying to repeat gets worse when it is repeated more.

acceptedIdeas: Fix the jump, land and collect cycle first, since every new level repeats it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Fix the jump, land and collect cycle first, since every new level repeats it

choices.label: Fix the jump, land and collect cycle first, since every new level repeats it
Add the levels, because more content gives players more reasons to carry on playing
Build the shop first, since an outer loop can stand in for the core loop

misconceptions.feedback: Each new level sends the player through the same stiff cycle again, so more content repeats a weak loop and does not mend it.
An outer loop gives the core loop a reason to repeat and does not replace it. The player still spends most of their time in the jump and collect cycle.

questions.prompt: In an invented rhythm game, a note scrolls down, the player taps in time, the game flashes 'Perfect' and adds to the score, and the next note scrolls down. After each song the player earns stars, and stars unlock new songs. Which part is an outer loop?
hints: The core loop is what the player repeats most often, and it lasts seconds.
Look for the cycle whose reward changes what the next pass of the core loop is like.
questions.onCorrect: Stars come once per song and open new songs, so the cycle is far longer than the loop of tapping notes and gives that loop a reason to repeat.

acceptedIdeas: Earning stars in a song to unlock new songs
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Earning stars in a song to unlock new songs

choices.label: Tapping a note in time and seeing 'Perfect' flash
The score rising after each tap
The next note scrolling down
Earning stars in a song to unlock new songs

misconceptions.feedback: That is the action and its feedback, repeated every few seconds, so it belongs to the core loop.
The score rises on every pass of the core loop, so it is the reward inside the loop. An outer loop is a longer cycle around it.
That returns the player to the first step of the core loop. An outer loop is a longer cycle that wraps around it.

questions.prompt: 'Players hoard a power-up until the last moment.' In MDA, this is a:
hints: Is it a rule, or something players do because of the rules?
A designer writes the rules directly, and behaviour like this appears only once people play.
questions.onCorrect: Hoarding is emergent behaviour: the rules only set the power-up's effect and cost.

acceptedIdeas: Dynamic
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Dynamic

choices.label: Aesthetic
Dynamic
Mechanic
Asset

misconceptions.feedback: The rule is what the power-up does. Hoarding it is a choice players make because of that rule.
An aesthetic is a feeling. Hoarding is an action players take.
An asset is something the game contains, such as a sound or a model. Hoarding is behaviour.

questions.prompt: Here are six statements about an invented card game called Ember Arena. In the lesson's terms, is each one a mechanic, a dynamic or an aesthetic?
hints: A mechanic is a rule or a number that the program checks, and a dynamic is something people do because of the rules.
An aesthetic is a feeling. Ask whether each statement describes a rule, a habit or an emotion.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The energy cost and the deck size are mechanics, holding the strongest card and copying the winning deck are dynamics, and the tension and the pride are aesthetics.

items.label: A card costs 3 energy and each turn gives 2 energy
items.explanation: It is a rule with numbers in it, which a program can check every turn.

items.label: Each deck holds exactly 30 cards
items.explanation: A fixed deck size is part of the rules and the data they work on.

items.label: Players hold their strongest card until the opponent has run out of energy
items.explanation: Nobody wrote it into the rules. It arises when people play with the energy rule.

items.label: Most players copy the one deck that wins early in the season
items.explanation: It is behaviour that emerges from play, and the rules do not mention it.

items.label: The tension when both players are down to 2 life
items.explanation: It is a feeling the player has, and a designer can only reach it by way of rules and play.

items.label: Pride at winning a game after being far behind
items.explanation: It is an emotional response, which is what the lesson means by an aesthetic.

questions.onCorrect: A designer writes only the mechanics. The dynamics and the feelings follow from them, so each has to be checked by watching people play.

questions.prompt: A game runs at 60 frames per second, so the screen is redrawn sixty times in each second. About how long does one frame last?
hints: A frame is one sixtieth of a second.
One second is 1000 milliseconds, shared out among the sixty frames.
questions.onCorrect: A frame is one sixtieth of a second, which is 16.7 ms to one decimal place. At 30 frames per second a frame lasts twice as long, 33.3 ms, and at 120 half as long, 8.3 ms.

acceptedIdeas: About 17 milliseconds
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 17 milliseconds

misconceptions.feedback: A second holds 1000 milliseconds, and those are shared among sixty frames. Each frame gets about ten times more than 1.7 milliseconds.
Sixty is the number of frames in a second, not the length of one. At 60 milliseconds a frame, only about 17 frames would fit in a second.
At 170 milliseconds a frame, only about six frames would fit in a second, far fewer than sixty.

choices.label: About 17 milliseconds
About 1.7 milliseconds
About 170 milliseconds
About 60 milliseconds

questions.prompt: A team wants a jump to start moving within 100 ms of the button press. In their 60 frames per second build the character first moves 7 frames after the press. By how many milliseconds does the build miss the target, to one decimal place?
hints: A frame at 60 frames per second lasts 1000 ÷ 60 milliseconds.
Seven frames of that length give the delay in milliseconds.
Compare that delay with the 100 ms target and say how far over it is.
questions.onCorrect: Seven frames last 116.7 ms, so the build is about one frame too slow. Cutting one frame of latency brings the delay to 100 ms.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One frame lasts 1000 ÷ 60 = 16.67 ms, so 7 frames last 116.7 ms, which is 16.7 ms over the 100 ms target.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole delay. The question asks by how much the delay goes over the 100 ms target.

questions.prompt: One frame lasts 16.67 ms and the delay is 4 frames. Which calculation gives the delay in milliseconds?
hints: Four frames of 16.7 ms each are four lots of 16.7 ms.
More frames make a longer delay, so the result has to be larger than 16.67.
questions.onCorrect: Frames times frame length gives milliseconds, and the reverse conversion divides.

misconceptions.feedback: Dividing the frame count by the length of a frame does not give a time. Division goes the other way, turning a delay in milliseconds into a number of frames.
That splits one frame's length into four parts, which is a quarter of a frame. The delay is made of four whole frames.

questions.prompt: At 60 frames per second a hit pauses the game for 2 frames. How long does the pause last?
hints: First find how long one frame lasts at 60 frames per second.
The pause is made of two of those frames, so which operation takes you from frames to milliseconds?
questions.onCorrect: Two frames of 16.67 ms each last 33.3 ms, a pause short enough to read as weight in the blow.

acceptedIdeas: About 33 ms
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 33 ms

choices.label: About 120 ms
About 33 ms
About 500 ms

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the 2 frames by 60, the frame rate. A frame lasts 1000 ÷ 60 ms, so 2 frames last 2 × 16.67 ms.
That divides 1000 ms by the 2 frames. The length of one frame comes from dividing 1000 ms by the frame rate, and the 2 frames are then multiplied by it.

questions.prompt: A sword hit sets off a large flash that covers the enemy, so the player cannot see its next move. Which word from this lesson names the problem?
hints: Which of the four words is about being able to read the screen?
Which word covers an effect that arrives on time and still hides what the player needs to see?
questions.onCorrect: The response arrives on time, but it hides the state the player needs, so extra effects can make a game worse.

acceptedIdeas: Legibility
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Legibility

choices.label: Anticipation
Latency
Legibility
Hit-stop

misconceptions.feedback: Anticipation is the wind-up before a blow, which tells the player something is about to happen. The flash comes after the hit and covers what the player needs to see.
Latency is the delay between a press and the response. Here the flash appears on time, and the trouble is what it hides.
Hit-stop is the short pause at the moment of impact, and it helps a blow feel heavy. The flash causes trouble by covering the screen, whatever pause comes with it.

questions.prompt: Testers keep saying the jump button ignored them at the edge of a ledge. Replays show they pressed jump 3 frames after the character ran off, and the character fell. Which change fits that cause?
hints: Compare the frame of the press with the frame at which the character left the ledge.
Which kind of forgiveness widens the time in which a press is still accepted after something has happened?
questions.onCorrect: A window of a few frames costs the game nothing, and players feel it as good control. Celeste's designers describe many tricks like this, each one fudged slightly in the player's favour.

acceptedIdeas: Keep accepting a jump for a few frames after the character leaves the ledge
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Keep accepting a jump for a few frames after the character leaves the ledge

choices.label: Keep accepting a jump for a few frames after the character leaves the ledge
Remember a jump pressed a few frames before landing and perform it on landing
Start the jump on the same frame as the press so the response comes sooner
Make the edge exact so only a press on the last frame on the ground counts

misconceptions.feedback: That is jump buffering, which Celeste uses for presses that come too early. These presses came too late, after the character had left the ledge.
The press came when the character was already in the air, so a quicker response would not help. What helps is a longer time in which a jump is accepted.
That removes forgiveness and players would miss more jumps. Coyote time does the opposite, by widening the window.

questions.prompt: A control responds 3 frames after the press. At 30 frames per second this delay is how many milliseconds longer than at 60 frames per second?
hints: Work out the delay in milliseconds at each frame rate.
A frame is longer at the lower frame rate.
Subtract the shorter delay from the longer one.
questions.onCorrect: The same code delay costs twice as much real time at half the frame rate, so response targets are better set in milliseconds.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At 30 fps three frames last 3 × 33.3 = 100 ms, at 60 fps they last 3 × 16.7 = 50 ms, and the difference is 50 ms.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the delay at 30 frames per second alone. The question asks for the difference between the two delays.
That is the delay in frames, and it is the same at both rates. Compare the times those frames take.

questions.prompt: A sword swing in an invented action game has these six parts. Which layer of feedback is each one: anticipation, impact or after-effect?
hints: Anticipation comes before contact, impact is the moment of contact, and the after-effect follows it.
For each item, ask whether the blow has landed yet.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The raised sword and the red eyes are anticipation, the 2 frame freeze and the clang are impact, and the screen shake and the fading ring are after-effects.

items.label: The hero raises the sword over her head for 4 frames before the swing
items.explanation: It is a wind-up that tells the player a blow is coming.

items.label: The enemy's eyes glow red just before it lunges
items.explanation: It warns the player before anything lands.

items.label: The game freezes for 2 frames at the moment the blade connects
items.explanation: A short pause at contact is hit-stop, which marks the moment of impact.

items.label: A sharp clang plays on the exact frame of contact
items.explanation: It is tied to the exact frame of contact.

items.label: The screen shakes for a quarter of a second after the hit
items.explanation: It follows the blow, so it is an after-effect.

items.label: The struck armour keeps ringing and the sound fades out
items.explanation: A sound that fades after contact is the tail of the response.

questions.onCorrect: Each layer has its own place in time. Anticipation warns, impact marks contact and the after-effect lets the blow fade, and any one of them can hide the others if it is too large.

questions.prompt: A team puts a screen flash, a screen shake, slow motion and a particle burst on every sword hit. Playtesters say the fights look great but they can no longer see the boss's next attack. What should the team do?
hints: Which of the four effects stay on screen after the blow has landed?
The lesson has a word for being able to read the state of the game at a glance.
questions.onCorrect: The effects arrive on time, so the trouble lies in what they hide. Keeping the short pause preserves the weight of the hit while the boss stays readable.

acceptedIdeas: Shorten or cut the effects that cover the boss and keep the brief pause at impact
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Shorten or cut the effects that cover the boss and keep the brief pause at impact

choices.label: Add one more audio cue to each hit, since another layer will make the hit easier to read
Shorten or cut the effects that cover the boss and keep the brief pause at impact
Remove the pause at impact, since it is the only effect that holds up the view
Keep every effect and tell players to watch the boss's feet for the next attack

misconceptions.feedback: A layer that hides the state of the game works against the others. An extra sound does not uncover what the flash is covering.
The pause is two frames or so, and it marks the moment of contact. What hides the boss is the flash and the particles that stay on screen after it.
Players should be able to read the game at a glance. Asking them to work around the effects leaves the legibility problem in place.

questions.prompt: A jump-buffer window is coded as 6 frames, which is 100 ms at 60 frames per second. The game is ported to 144 frames per second with the code unchanged. How long is the window now, in milliseconds to one decimal place?
hints: Find how long one frame lasts at 144 frames per second.
The code still counts 6 frames, so multiply that frame length by 6.
Compare the result with the 100 ms the window used to give.
questions.onCorrect: The same 6 frames now cover 41.7 ms, less than half of what players had. Windows set in milliseconds keep their size when the frame rate changes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At 144 frames per second one frame lasts 1000 ÷ 144 = 6.94 ms, so 6 frames last 41.7 ms.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the window at 60 frames per second. At 144 frames per second a frame is shorter, so 6 frames last less time.

questions.prompt: A player has cleared every level of world 1 without dying, and world 2 plays just like world 1. Using the flow model, what will the player most likely feel as world 2 goes on?
hints: Compare the player's skill after world 1 with the challenge of world 2.
In the model, which state has the challenge far below the skill?
questions.onCorrect: The same level that once held the player's attention now asks less of them, because the skill has moved and the challenge has not.

acceptedIdeas: Boredom, since their skill has risen and the challenge has stayed where it was
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Boredom, since their skill has risen and the challenge has stayed where it was

choices.label: Boredom, since their skill has risen and the challenge has stayed where it was
Anxiety, since a new world always feels more demanding than the last one did
Flow, since levels the player can already clear are the ones they enjoy most

misconceptions.feedback: Anxiety comes when the challenge is far above the player's skill. Here the challenge has stayed the same while the skill rose, so the gap runs the other way.
Flow needs the challenge to sit close to the skill. A level cleared without effort sits below the channel, which is boredom.

questions.prompt: A designer builds one wave of a platformer from four levels. In what order should they come?
hints: A player has to meet a skill before they are tested on it.
Which level gives the player a rest, and what does it need to follow?

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The first level teaches the jump, the second tests it by chaining three, the third adds a twist with a moving platform, and the quiet room gives relief before the next wave starts higher.

items: A first level introduces a single jump
A second level chains three of those jumps
A third level adds a moving platform to the jumps
A quiet room with no new demand

questions.onCorrect: Teach, test, twist and relief give the wave its shape. The next wave starts higher than this one did, so the line falls at the end of each wave and still rises overall.

questions.prompt: A player of skill 8 meets a level of challenge 3. In the flow model, which state is the player in?
hints: The challenge is far below the skill.
At skill 8 the channel covers challenges from 7 to 9. Where does 3 sit against that range?
questions.onCorrect: Challenge far below skill puts the player under the channel, where nothing is demanded.

acceptedIdeas: Boredom
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Boredom

misconceptions.feedback: Anxiety is the opposite case, where the challenge is far above the skill.
Flow needs the challenge to lie inside the channel around the skill, which at skill 8 runs from 7 to 9, and 3 is well below it.

choices.label: Anxiety
Flow
Boredom

questions.prompt: A shooter counts how often the player dies on each level. After three deaths in a row it quietly lowers the enemies' accuracy. What does the lesson call this approach to difficulty? Give the name or its initials.
hints: Who changes the difficulty here, the designer, the player or the game?
Of the three approaches in the lesson, which one measures how the player is doing?
questions.onCorrect: The other two approaches are set before play begins, by the designer or by the player, while this one changes during play.

acceptedIdeas: dynamic difficulty adjustment
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Dynamic difficulty adjustment, because the game changes its challenge in response to measured play.

misconceptions.feedback: Rubber-banding is the racing-game case, where trailing cars are sped up. The general name for a game changing its challenge from measured play is dynamic difficulty adjustment.
Selectable difficulty is chosen by the player before play begins. Here the game itself changes the challenge from what it measures.
Fixed difficulty gives every player the same curve. This game changes its challenge for one player after measuring how they do.

questions.prompt: An enemy starts with 200 health. Each time the player dies three times in a row, the game cuts the enemy's health by 10 percent of its current value. What is the enemy's health after two such adjustments?
hints: Each cut is 10 percent of the current value, so the cut gets smaller.
After one adjustment the enemy has 90 percent of its health.
Take 90 percent of the new value for the second adjustment.
questions.onCorrect: Because every cut applies to the current health, two cuts of 10 percent remove 38 points, not 40.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first adjustment gives 200 × 0.9 = 180, and the second gives 180 × 0.9 = 162.

misconceptions.feedback: That takes 10 percent of the original 200 twice. The second cut applies to the reduced health.
That is the health after one adjustment. The question asks about two.

questions.prompt: A card game gives the player who is behind an extra card each turn. In testing, the lead keeps changing hands and nobody stays far ahead for long. What does the extra card do?
hints: Ask whether the effect of the extra card adds to the gap or works against it.
Compare it with rubber-banding in a racing game.
questions.onCorrect: A negative feedback loop pulls players back together, which keeps a comeback possible, while a positive loop would let an early lead snowball.

acceptedIdeas: It acts as a negative feedback loop, since falling behind brings a push back towards level
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It acts as a negative feedback loop, since falling behind brings a push back towards level

choices.label: It acts as a positive feedback loop, since the trailing player is being given a reward
It acts as a negative feedback loop, since falling behind brings a push back towards level
It makes the result random, so the lead changes by chance and the rule has no say

misconceptions.feedback: A positive loop strengthens whatever set it off, as when a lead earns the power to extend itself. Here falling behind brings help that shrinks the gap.
The extra card follows a rule that depends on the score, so it is not chance. A rule that answers the gap between players is a feedback loop.

questions.prompt: In the lesson's model a challenge within 1 point of the player's skill is flow, a higher challenge is anxiety and a lower one is boredom. Six invented players meet a level. What does each one feel?
hints: For each player, subtract the skill from the challenge.
A difference between minus 1 and 1 is flow, a larger positive one is anxiety and a larger negative one is boredom.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Skill 3 with challenge 7 and skill 2 with challenge 5 are anxiety, skill 5 with challenge 6 and skill 7 with challenge 7 are flow, and skill 8 with challenge 3 and skill 9 with challenge 7 are boredom.

items.label: Skill 3 meets challenge 7
items.explanation: The challenge is 4 points above the skill, well beyond the channel.

items.label: Skill 2 meets challenge 5
items.explanation: The challenge is 3 points above the skill, outside the 1 point channel.

items.label: Skill 5 meets challenge 6
items.explanation: The challenge is 1 point above the skill, which is inside the channel.

items.label: Skill 7 meets challenge 7
items.explanation: Challenge and skill match, so the player is in the middle of the channel.

items.label: Skill 8 meets challenge 3
items.explanation: The challenge is 5 points below the skill, far under the channel.

items.label: Skill 9 meets challenge 7
items.explanation: The challenge is 2 points below the skill, so it falls outside the channel.

questions.onCorrect: The channel is narrow, so a level that suits one player is too hard for another and too easy for a third.

questions.prompt: A designer makes each later boss harder by doubling its health and damage and changing nothing else. Testers who have mastered the fights call them tedious, while newer players keep losing. What does the wave curve suggest instead?
hints: Compare what a doubled boss asks of the player with what the original boss asked.
The wave in the lesson changes what the player has to do as well as how much of it.
questions.onCorrect: A harder level should ask for something new, such as a twist, and then give the player room to settle. A bigger number alone repeats the same ask.

acceptedIdeas: Add a new demand at the top of each wave and follow it with a relief level
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Add a new demand at the top of each wave and follow it with a relief level

choices.label: Double the numbers again, since the testers say the fights are still too easy
Let each player pick a multiplier at the start, so nobody meets a fight at the wrong level
Add a new demand at the top of each wave and follow it with a relief level

misconceptions.feedback: Bigger numbers stretch the same demand. Players who have mastered it stay bored and the players still learning it stay anxious.
That is selectable difficulty, and it leaves the fights as the same demand with bigger numbers. Not every player chooses well either.

questions.prompt: A sword hits for 50 damage, and one hit in ten is a critical hit that does triple damage. Roughly how much damage does a hit do on average?
hints: Most hits are ordinary hits.
A critical hit does 100 more than an ordinary hit, but it happens only one time in ten.
questions.onCorrect: Only one hit in ten is critical, so the average is pulled a little above the ordinary 50 and no further.

acceptedIdeas: A little more than 50, since only one hit in ten is critical
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A little more than 50, since only one hit in ten is critical

choices.label: About 150, since a critical hit does triple damage when it lands
About 100, since the average of 50 and 150 is halfway between them
A little more than 50, since only one hit in ten is critical
Exactly 50, since a critical hit is too rare to change the average

misconceptions.feedback: 150 is the damage of a critical hit alone, and only one hit in ten is critical. The other nine do 50.
100 would be about right only if ordinary and critical hits were equally common. Nine hits in ten are ordinary, so the average stays much nearer 50.
One hit in ten does 150, which is 100 more than an ordinary hit, so the average must lie above 50 even though most single hits do exactly 50.

questions.prompt: A sword hits for 50 damage. It misses 30 percent of the time, and 10 percent of its hits are critical hits that do 150. What is the expected damage per swing?
hints: Find the probability of each of the three outcomes.
A critical hit needs a hit first, so multiply 0.7 by 0.1.
Add each probability times its damage.
questions.onCorrect: A miss chance multiplies the whole expected value by the chance of hitting, so 60 × 0.7 gives the same result.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A miss does 0, a plain hit has probability 0.7 × 0.9 = 0.63 and does 50, and a critical hit has probability 0.7 × 0.1 = 0.07 and does 150, so 0 + 31.5 + 10.5 = 42.

misconceptions.feedback: That ignores the misses. Three swings in ten do nothing.
That is the damage of a plain hit. Weight the plain hit, the crit and the miss by their probabilities.

questions.prompt: An enemy has 240 health. A weapon does 40 damage per hit and hits 3 times per second. How long does it take to kill the enemy?
hints: First find the damage per second: damage per hit times hits per second.
Then ask how many of those seconds it takes to use up the health.
questions.onCorrect: At 120 damage per second the 240 health lasts 2 seconds.

acceptedIdeas: 2 seconds
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 2 seconds

choices.label: 6 seconds
0.5 seconds
2 seconds

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the health by the damage per hit, which counts hits. Divide by the damage per second, 40 × 3 = 120.
That divides the damage per second by the health, which is upside down. Time to kill is the health divided by the damage per second.

questions.prompt: A designer compares two upgrade prices. Plan A costs 100 + 60 × (level − 1). Plan B costs 100 × 1.4^(level − 1). At which level does plan B first cost more than plan A?
hints: Work out both prices for level 2, then level 3, and keep going level by level.
At level 2 plan B is the cheaper of the two, because 1.4 adds only 40 percent of 100.
Stop at the first level where plan B's price is higher than plan A's.
questions.onCorrect: Plan B costs less at levels 2, 3 and 4 and more from level 5 on, and the gap keeps widening. A price that multiplies overtakes a fixed step sooner or later, so designers check the later levels.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Plan A costs 100, 160, 220, 280 and 340 at levels 1 to 5, and plan B costs 100, 140, 196, 274.4 and 384.16, so plan B first passes plan A at level 5.

misconceptions.feedback: At level 4 plan B costs 274.4 and plan A costs 280, so plan B has not passed it yet.

questions.prompt: Players earn 500 coins an hour, and the shops and repair bills take back 350 an hour. After a week of play the best items cost only a few minutes of earnings. What is happening, and what fixes it?
hints: Compare how many coins enter the game each hour with how many leave it.
The lesson has a word for what happens when the sources exceed the sinks.
questions.onCorrect: A surplus of 150 coins an hour grows every hour. Either more coins have to leave through new sinks or fewer have to arrive.

acceptedIdeas: Inflation, since sources exceed sinks, so add sinks or trim the sources
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Inflation, since sources exceed sinks, so add sinks or trim the sources

choices.label: Deflation, since players hold too few coins, so raise the rewards to refill their purses
Nothing, since a pile of coins shows that players like the economy
Inflation, since sources exceed sinks, so add sinks or trim the sources

misconceptions.feedback: Players gain 150 coins more than they spend every hour, so too many coins are entering the game. Raising the rewards would make it worse.
Coins that nothing can absorb make prices lose their meaning, and players have nothing left to work towards.

questions.prompt: A boss drops a rare item on 5 percent of kills, and every kill is independent of the others. What is the probability that a player kills it 20 times and sees no drop, as a percentage to one decimal place?
hints: Each kill has a 0.95 chance of giving no drop.
When independent events must all happen, their probabilities are multiplied.
Multiply 0.95 by itself once for each of the 20 kills.
questions.onCorrect: About one player in three has nothing after 20 kills, although the chance is 5 percent on every kill. Designers who mind that add a limit that raises the chance or guarantees the drop after a set run of misses.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each kill misses the drop with probability 0.95, and independent events multiply, so the chance of 20 misses is 0.95^20 = 0.358, which is 35.8 percent.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance of a drop on one kill. The question asks about 20 kills in a row with no drop.
That is the chance of at least one drop in 20 kills. The question asks for no drop at all.

questions.prompt: After 60 kills of a boss, many players still lack a 2 percent drop. The designer says every kill is independent, so the 61st still has a 2 percent chance and nothing is wrong. About 30 percent of players are in that position. What is the best response?
hints: Work out how likely 60 misses in a row are, with a 98 percent chance of a miss each time.
Think about a change that helps the unlucky players without making the item common.
questions.onCorrect: A chance of 0.98 per kill gives 0.98^60, about 30 percent, so the complaint is real. A pity counter cuts off the worst runs of bad luck.

acceptedIdeas: Add a pity rule that guarantees the drop after a run of misses
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Add a pity rule that guarantees the drop after a run of misses

choices.label: Add a pity rule that guarantees the drop after a run of misses
Tell players the drop is due soon, since rolls even out over a long run
Raise the rate to 20 percent for everyone, so that waiting stays short

misconceptions.feedback: Each kill is independent, so earlier misses do not make the next kill any likelier. Believing the roll is due is the gambler's fallacy.
At 20 percent the item is no longer rare. A pity rule limits the longest waits and keeps the ordinary rate low.

questions.prompt: An enemy has 360 health. Weapon A does 90 damage per hit, hits once a second and never misses. Weapon B does 45 damage per hit, hits 3 times a second and misses 25 percent of the time. By how many seconds does weapon B kill the enemy sooner, to two decimal places?
hints: Expected damage per second is the damage per hit times the hits per second times the chance of a hit.
Time to kill is the health divided by the damage per second, for each weapon.
Subtract the shorter time from the longer one.
questions.onCorrect: Weapon B kills in about 3.56 seconds against 4 for weapon A, even though each of its hits does half the damage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Weapon A does 90 per second, so it takes 360 ÷ 90 = 4 seconds. Weapon B does 45 × 3 × 0.75 = 101.25 per second, so it takes 360 ÷ 101.25 = 3.56 seconds, which is 0.44 seconds sooner.

misconceptions.feedback: That is weapon B's time to kill. The question asks how much sooner that is than weapon A's 4 seconds.

questions.prompt: An invented dungeon game moves coins in these six ways. Is each one a source, where coins enter the game, or a sink, where they leave it?
hints: A source adds coins to what players hold, and a sink takes coins out of the game.
Ask for each item whether the player's purse grows or shrinks.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The quest, the goblin drops and the login bonus are sources, and the repair bill, the sword and the bag upgrade are sinks.

items.label: A quest pays 120 coins
items.explanation: Coins enter the game and land in the player's purse.

items.label: Slain goblins drop coins
items.explanation: Coins are created by a monster dying, so they enter the game.

items.label: A daily login gives 50 coins
items.explanation: It adds coins without taking any away.

items.label: Armour repairs cost 80 coins
items.explanation: The coins are paid out and leave the game.

items.label: A shop sells a sword for 300 coins
items.explanation: The player's coins go to the shop and are removed from play.

items.label: An upgrade to the player's bag costs 500 coins
items.explanation: The coins leave the economy in exchange for the upgrade.

questions.onCorrect: A designer tracks both lists together, because a game whose sources exceed its sinks inflates and one whose sinks exceed its sources leaves players unable to buy anything.

questions.prompt: A designer wants a card game to last 8 rounds. In a paper test each player starts with 12 coins, earns 1 coin each round and then pays 3 coins for a card. In which round does a player first fail to afford the card?
hints: Each round the player's coins change by +1 and then by −3. What is the change over a whole round?
Keep a running total round by round, remembering that the player earns before they pay.
Find the first round in which the coins in hand, after earning, are fewer than 3.
questions.onCorrect: The economy runs dry in round 7, one round before the game should end. The designer can lower the cost, raise the income or shorten the game, and then test again.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A player has 12 − 2 × 5 = 2 coins after five rounds, so in round 6 they earn 1, hold 3 and pay 3, ending on 0. In round 7 they earn 1, hold 1 and cannot pay 3.

misconceptions.feedback: In round 6 the player starts with 2 coins, earns 1 to hold 3, and can still pay 3. The first round with too few coins is the next one.
The game is meant to last 8 rounds, but the coins run out before then, in an earlier round.

questions.prompt: The share kept at any step is the players who got through it divided by which group?
hints: Which players had the chance to get through the step?
A share is a part divided by the whole group that it was taken from.
questions.onCorrect: Only players who reached a step could have got through it, so they are the right denominator.

acceptedIdeas: The players who reached that step
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The players who reached that step

misconceptions.feedback: That is the base for the tutorial only, since everyone who starts has reached it. Level 1 could be tried only by the 150 who got past the tutorial.
Those are the players the step lost. The share kept sets the players who got through against everyone who had the chance to.

choices.label: The players who started the game
The players who reached that step
The players who left at that step

questions.prompt: A designer eases level 2 and changes nothing else. A new group of 200 players gives 150 through the tutorial, 100 through level 1 and 70 through level 2. Level 1 kept 60 percent before and keeps about 67 percent now. What should the designer conclude about level 1?
hints: Ask what, if anything, was changed at level 1 between the two groups.
Compare the seven point move at level 1 with the twenty point move at level 2.
questions.onCorrect: The share at level 2 rose from 50 to 70 percent, far more than the drift at a level nobody touched, so the easing is credited with that gain and level 1 is left as it was.

acceptedIdeas: Nothing yet, since level 1 was untouched and groups of this size vary between runs
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Nothing yet, since level 1 was untouched and groups of this size vary between runs

choices.label: The change to level 2 must also have helped level 1, so the team should credit it for that
Nothing yet, since level 1 was untouched and groups of this size vary between runs
Level 1 is fixed now, so the team can stop testing it and move on to level 3

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing about level 1 was changed, so the easing at level 2 gives no reason for it to improve. A couple of hundred players per group vary by several points from run to run.
A move of about seven points on an untouched level is the kind of difference two groups can show by chance, so it does not mean level 1 was fixed.

questions.prompt: 400 players started, 300 finished the tutorial and 120 beat level 1. What percentage of the players who reached level 1 beat it?
hints: Find how many players reached level 1.
Those players are the ones who finished the tutorial, not the 400 who started.
Divide the 120 who beat level 1 by that number and turn the fraction into a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Shares of those who reached each step show where a design loses players, and the counts alone do not.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 120 of the 300 who finished the tutorial beat level 1, and 120 ÷ 300 = 0.4, which is 40 percent.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by the 400 who started. Divide by those who finished the tutorial.
That is the count, not a percentage.

questions.prompt: After a playtest, three of five players say they would like a map. The designer watched all five wander for over a minute near the same door in level 2. What should the designer do first?
hints: Which is the stronger evidence, what the players said or what all five did?
Think about what a map would fix and what it would leave in place.
questions.onCorrect: A minute spent wandering is an exact finding, and it points at the door. A request for a map is the players' guess at a cure.

acceptedIdeas: Find out what made players miss the door, since a map is only one possible fix
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Find out what made players miss the door, since a map is only one possible fix

choices.label: Find out what made players miss the door, since a map is only one possible fix
Add the map, since players asked for it and they know best what they need
Ask the players to sketch the level they would build, since they know it best

misconceptions.feedback: Players can report that they got lost, and they are poor at naming the fix. Watching showed where and why, and the cause may be a door that is hard to see.
That hands design work to people who have just met the game. A playtest question should be one that watching can answer, such as where players lose the way.

questions.prompt: A team wants to fix a level that players keep failing. In what order should it do these five things?
hints: A prototype is built to answer a question, so which comes first?
A change can only be credited if it is tested on players who did not see the old version.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The team starts from a question, builds the smallest prototype that can answer it, watches new players, changes one thing about the weakest step and tests with a new group.

items: Write down one question the test has to answer
Build the smallest prototype that can answer it
Watch new players in silence and note what they do
Change one thing about the weakest step
Test the change with a new group of players

questions.onCorrect: Each step needs the one before it. The question decides what the prototype contains, the watching decides what to change, and a new group tests the change on its own.

questions.prompt:
A ball is moved by this loop, which runs once per frame.

`while playing:`
    `ball_x += 5`
    `draw()`

A tester on a 144 Hz display with vsync says the ball is much faster than on a 60 Hz laptop. What explains it?
hints: How many times does the loop run in one second on each machine?
Multiply the step by the number of passes to get pixels per second on each display.
questions.onCorrect: The code is the same on both machines and the game is not, because the speed depends on how fast the loop happens to run.

acceptedIdeas: Each pass moves the ball 5 pixels, so 144 passes a second cover 720 pixels against 300 at 60
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each pass moves the ball 5 pixels, so 144 passes a second cover 720 pixels against 300 at 60

choices.label: Rounding errors grow faster at 144 Hz, so the ball drifts further each second than at 60 Hz
Each pass moves the ball 5 pixels, so 144 passes a second cover 720 pixels against 300 at 60
The faster display makes each 5 pixel step larger on screen, so the ball seems to move faster

misconceptions.feedback: Rounding error exists in games that vary the step, but it is far too small to make a ball more than twice as fast. The speed follows from the number of passes.
A step is 5 pixels on any display. What changes is how many steps happen each second, since the loop has no clock.

questions.prompt: The step is 20 ms. A frame takes 110 ms and the lag starts at 0. How many updates run?
hints: Add the frame time to the lag.
Count how many whole steps of 20 ms fit in the lag.
110 ÷ 20 gives a whole part and a remainder.
questions.onCorrect: The remainder is not lost: it stays in the accumulator and counts towards the next frame.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The lag is 110 ms, and each update spends 20 ms, so 5 updates run (100 ms) and 10 ms remain.

misconceptions.feedback: That rounds 110 ÷ 20 up. An update runs only when a whole step of 20 ms is available.
Updates come in whole steps. Count the whole steps in the lag.

questions.prompt: In the worked frames of 30, 50 and 10 ms the first frame leaves 10 ms of lag after its update. Why is that 10 ms kept for the next frame?
hints: Ask what would happen to the simulation's clock if the 10 ms were thrown away every frame.
Every update is exactly one step long. Where else could the leftover time be spent?
questions.onCorrect: Time that is dropped would let the simulation fall behind the clock a little more every frame, so the loop carries it forward.

acceptedIdeas: It is real time the simulation has not yet covered, so a later frame has to spend it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is real time the simulation has not yet covered, so a later frame has to spend it

choices.label: The next update has to be longer than 20 ms, so that the game keeps its overall speed
The renderer needs it to draw the frame, and the updates cannot make any use of it
It is real time the simulation has not yet covered, so a later frame has to spend it

misconceptions.feedback: Every update advances the world by exactly 20 ms. The leftover is spent by adding it to the next frame's time, which sometimes buys one more update.
The renderer reads the lag to place the picture between updates, but the updates use it too. It joins the next frame's time and pays for later updates.

questions.prompt: The step is 20 ms and the lag starts at 0. Frames take 70, 25, 5 and 40 ms in turn. How many updates run in total over the four frames?
hints: Add each frame's time to the lag left by the one before, and take away 20 ms for every update.
The total real time is 140 ms. How many whole steps of 20 ms is that, and what is left?
questions.onCorrect: The frames bring 140 ms in all, and 7 steps of 20 ms use it exactly, so nothing is left in the lag at the end.

acceptedIdeas: 7 updates
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 7 updates

choices.label: 7 updates
6 updates
9 updates

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the whole updates in each frame separately, 3 + 1 + 0 + 2, and drops the time each frame leaves behind. The leftovers add up to one more update.
That rounds each frame up to whole updates, 4 + 2 + 1 + 2. The loop runs an update only when a full 20 ms is waiting.

questions.prompt: The previous update put an object at x = 100 and the latest at x = 120. The step is 20 ms and the lag is 5 ms. At what x is the object drawn?
hints: Divide the lag by the step to get a fraction.
The fraction is between 0 and 1.
Go that fraction of the way from 100 to 120.
questions.onCorrect: Drawing between the two updates lets the picture move smoothly even when the update rate and the frame rate do not match.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The fraction is 5 ÷ 20 = 0.25, so the drawn position is 100 + 0.25 × (120 − 100) = 105.

misconceptions.feedback: That draws the latest update. A frame is drawn part of the way between the last two.
That uses a fraction of one half, from 10 ms of lag. Divide the actual lag by the step.

questions.prompt: The step is 20 ms and a frame stalls for 500 ms. The loop caps the frame time at 250 ms before adding it to the lag, which starts at 0. How many updates run?
hints: Apply the cap before adding the frame to the lag.
The lag cannot exceed 250 ms.
Count the whole steps of 20 ms in 250 ms.
questions.onCorrect: Without the cap the loop would try to run 25 updates, and if each took long enough the lag would never shrink.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The frame time is capped at 250 ms, and 250 ÷ 20 = 12.5, so 12 updates run and 10 ms remain.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the whole 500 ms, which the cap does not allow.
That rounds 250 ÷ 20 up. Updates run only for whole steps.

questions.prompt:
A programmer wrote the fixed timestep loop with an `if` where the lesson has a `while`.

`lag += frame_ms`
`if lag >= 20:`
    `update()`
    `lag -= 20`

Over four frames of 70, 25, 5 and 40 ms, only 4 updates run and 60 ms of lag is left. What do players see?
hints: Count how many updates a 70 ms frame needs and how many the `if` allows.
Time that has passed and has not been simulated is the lag. What happens to the game's clock while the lag grows?
questions.onCorrect: A `while` keeps running updates until the lag is below one step, and an `if` runs one at most. After a stall the `while` catches up and the `if` does not.

acceptedIdeas: The game falls behind the clock and runs in slow motion until frames get short
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The game falls behind the clock and runs in slow motion until frames get short

choices.label: The world jumps ahead of the clock, since the leftover time is counted twice over
The game falls behind the clock and runs in slow motion until frames get short
Nothing, since the extra lag is cleared as soon as each frame has been drawn

misconceptions.feedback: Fewer updates run than the time calls for, so the world runs behind the clock. Nothing counts any time twice.
Only updates take time out of the lag, and one update a frame cannot keep up after a long frame. The 60 ms stays and grows while frames stay long.

questions.prompt: In the fixed timestep loop, in what order do these four things happen within one frame?
hints: The lag has to hold the new time before anything can be spent.
Drawing comes once the simulation has caught up as far as it can.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The frame's time goes into the lag first, the loop checks whether a step is waiting, each update takes one step off the lag, and the frame is drawn once the lag is below a step.

items: Add the time the last frame took to the lag
Check that the lag is at least one step
Run one update and take one step off the lag
Draw the frame between the last two updates

questions.onCorrect: The updates come between the lag growing and the picture being drawn, and the check repeats until less than one step is waiting.

questions.prompt: A game moves objects by speed × delta time on every frame. What problem can remain?
hints: Think about what happens when a frame takes much longer than usual.
A ball moves speed × delta time in each step. How far does it move when one frame takes a long time?
questions.onCorrect: Scaling by delta time keeps average speed but not the path taken, which depends on the size of each step.

acceptedIdeas: Fast objects can still pass through thin walls
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Fast objects can still pass through thin walls

choices.label: Objects move more slowly on faster machines
Objects stop moving whenever the frame time changes
The game cannot draw more than 60 frames per second
Fast objects can still pass through thin walls

misconceptions.feedback: Scaling by delta time keeps the distance per second the same, so the speed does not fall on faster machines.
Objects keep moving. The step they move by changes with the frame time.
Scaling movement by delta time has no bearing on the render rate.

questions.prompt: A character has the flags `isJumping`, `isDucking` and `isDiving`. A bug report says its hitbox shrinks to the ducking size in the middle of a jump. What does this show about the flags?
hints: Can `isJumping` and `isDucking` both be true at the same time in this code?
Think about how many combinations three flags allow and how many of them describe something the character can really do.
questions.onCorrect: Three flags allow eight combinations and only four make sense. The state machine removes the other four by naming the real states.

acceptedIdeas: Nothing stops two flags being true together, so code must guard against impossible states
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Nothing stops two flags being true together, so code must guard against impossible states

choices.label: The jump code lacks one check that is easy to add, so the flags themselves are not at fault
Nothing stops two flags being true together, so code must guard against impossible states
Three flags are too few, and a fourth flag, `isStanding`, would stop the clash

misconceptions.feedback: Adding the check fixes this case, but every other place that reads the flags needs the same guard, and each new flag needs more.
A fourth flag doubles the combinations from 8 to 16 and still does not stop two flags being true at once.

questions.prompt: The designer adds an `isStunned` flag, and now nothing else should work while the character is stunned. In the flag version of the code, where does that rule go?
hints: Which pieces of code read `isJumping` and `isDucking` today?
Think about what would stop the jump code from running during a stun.
questions.onCorrect: Each new rule becomes one more condition at every place that reads the flags. A state machine holds the rule once, in the transition table.

acceptedIdeas: Into every place that reads a flag, each of which must also check `isStunned`
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Into every place that reads a flag, each of which must also check `isStunned`

choices.label: Into the flag alone, since the other flags are ignored whenever it is true
Into the setter, which clears the other flags whenever `isStunned` is set to true
Into every place that reads a flag, each of which must also check `isStunned`

misconceptions.feedback: Setting a flag does not stop other code from reading `isJumping` or `isDucking` and acting on them. Each reader has to check for the stun.
Clearing the flags loses what the character was doing, so nothing knows what to return to when the stun ends. A jump key press can also set a flag again while stunned.

questions.prompt:
This transition table drives a character.

`TABLE = {`
    `('standing', 'jump'): 'jumping',`
    `('standing', 'duck'): 'ducking',`
    `('jumping', 'duck'): 'diving',`
    `('jumping', 'land'): 'standing',`
    `('ducking', 'release'): 'standing',`
`}`
`state = TABLE.get((state, event), state)`

A player jumps, ducks to dive, lands, then presses jump. The character stays in the diving pose and ignores every key. Which entry is missing?
hints: Follow the events through the table one at a time and write down the state after each.
Which event has no entry for the state the character is in when it lands?
questions.onCorrect: A missing entry means the event is ignored, so the machine stays in diving. The table makes the gap easy to see, because every state and event pair is either handled or visibly ignored.

acceptedIdeas: `('diving', 'land'): 'standing'`
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `('diving', 'land'): 'standing'`

choices.label: `('diving', 'land'): 'standing'`
`('diving', 'jump'): 'jumping'`
`('standing', 'land'): 'standing'`
`('ducking', 'land'): 'standing'`

misconceptions.feedback: That would let the player jump out of a dive, which is a different rule. The player landed, and landing is the event that has to end a dive.
The character is in diving when it lands, so a row for standing never runs. The entry has to start from diving.
The character is diving when it lands, so a row for ducking never runs. A dive starts from a jump, and the missing entry starts from diving.

questions.prompt: An event arrives in a state whose row has no entry for it. What does the machine do?
hints: Think about what an empty cell in the table says about that pair of state and event.
The lesson says an empty cell means the event does nothing in that state.
questions.onCorrect: A missing entry means that event does nothing in that state, so the machine stays where it is.

acceptedIdeas: It stays in the state it is in
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It stays in the state it is in

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing in the table sends the machine back to a first state. A missing entry sends it nowhere.
A missing entry is not a fault. The empty cell is itself a rule, and it covers that pair of state and event.

choices.label: It goes back to the first state
It stays in the state it is in
It stops with an error

questions.prompt: The character starts as standing and receives the events jump, duck, release, land. Release has no entry for the diving state. Which state is it in at the end?
hints: Follow each event from the current state, using the table.
Write down the state after each of the four events, one at a time.
questions.onCorrect: Release does nothing while diving, and land then returns the character to standing.

acceptedIdeas: Standing
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Standing

misconceptions.feedback: Land has an entry for diving, which moves the character out of it. Follow all four events.
Jumping is where the first event leads, but three more events follow it.
Release would end a duck from the ducking state, but the character was diving by then.

choices.label: Diving
Jumping
Standing
Ducking

questions.prompt: Four ground states, standing, walking, running and ducking, each handle jump and attack in the same way. The designer adds a fifth, sliding, that must do the same. How many new arrows does that need?
hints: In a flat machine each state needs its own arrow for each event it handles.
In a hierarchy the parent holds the arrow once for all of its substates.
questions.onCorrect: The saving grows with every state added, which is why large machines use a hierarchy.

acceptedIdeas: Two in a flat machine, and none if sliding joins a parent
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Two in a flat machine, and none if sliding joins a parent

choices.label: Two either way, since every state needs arrows of its own to handle events
Two in a flat machine, and none if sliding joins a parent
One in a flat machine, and one with a parent state

misconceptions.feedback: A state inside a parent inherits the parent's arrows, so sliding gets jump and attack from it without any arrows of its own.
A flat machine needs an arrow for each of the two events, which is two. With a parent state sliding needs none.

questions.prompt: A machine moves a character from ducking to standing. In what order do these four things happen?
hints: An event has to arrive before anything moves.
`exit` and `enter` run once at the transition, and `update` runs on every tick after it.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The release event arrives first, `exit` clears what the ducking state set up, `enter` sets up standing, and `update` then runs on every tick while the character is standing.

items: The release event arrives while the character is ducking
The ducking state's `exit` method runs
The standing state's `enter` method runs
The standing state's `update` method runs on each tick

questions.onCorrect: Setup and cleanup run once at the transition, so neither has to be repeated every frame in `update`.

questions.prompt: A character is hit and stunned for half a second. When the stun ends it should go back to whatever it was doing, which might have been ducking, running or jumping. Which extension of the state machine fits?
hints: The machine has to remember the state the character was in before the stun.
Which extension in the lesson brings back what was underneath, as closing a menu does?
questions.onCorrect: The stun is pushed onto the stack, and popping it returns the character to the state it left, whichever that was.

acceptedIdeas: A pushdown stack, which puts the stun on top and pops it to resume the earlier state
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A pushdown stack, which puts the stun on top and pops it to resume the earlier state

choices.label: A parent state called on the ground, so that every ground state shares the stun transition
One more flag, `wasDucking`, set before the stun and read after it
A pushdown stack, which puts the stun on top and pops it to resume the earlier state

misconceptions.feedback: A parent state shares transitions among its substates, and it does not remember which substate the character was in. The stun has to remember what lies underneath it.
That covers ducking only, and running and jumping would each need a flag of their own. A stack remembers whichever state was underneath.

questions.prompt: A game saves each match as a list of commands with the frame at which each was issued. Replaying a list on the same machine gives a different result from the match itself. Which cause fits?
hints: A replay feeds the same commands to a fresh game at the same frames. What has to be true of the game for the result to match?
Recall which loop from the earlier lesson makes a given sequence of inputs give the same result on every machine.
questions.onCorrect: A recording replays only if the game responds to the same commands in the same way each time, which is why the fixed timestep matters.

acceptedIdeas: The game is not deterministic, for example because its step varies with frame time
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The game is not deterministic, for example because its step varies with frame time

choices.label: The game is not deterministic, for example because its step varies with frame time
The list is too short, since the frames between the commands were never recorded at all
Commands cannot be replayed, since a command is gone as soon as it has run

misconceptions.feedback: A list of commands describes a match completely when the game is deterministic. Recording every frame would multiply the size and still would not fix a game that answers the same commands differently.
A command is an object, and it is kept after it has run. That is what makes recording and replay possible.

questions.prompt: A game stores the commands a player executes so that they can be undone. Commands A, B, C and D are executed in that order, and the player then undoes twice. Which commands are still applied?
hints: Each undo reverses one command.
Which command does an undo reverse first, the oldest or the most recent?
questions.onCorrect: C and D are not deleted yet: they sit in a redo list until a new command is executed.

acceptedIdeas: A and B
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A and B

misconceptions.feedback: That is the result of undoing once. Two undos reverse two commands, so one more has gone than this.
Undo reverses the most recent command first, so D goes first and then C. The oldest commands are the ones that stay applied.
That is the state before any undo. Each undo reverses one command, so after two undos two commands are no longer applied.

choices.label: A, B and C
A and B
C and D
A, B, C and D

questions.prompt: A level editor lets players undo and redo. A player undoes three steps, makes a different change, then presses redo. The editor applies an old step on top of the new change and leaves a layout that was never built. What did the editor forget to do?
hints: After the player makes a different change, does the old future still follow from the new history?
Which list holds the steps that were undone and could be done again?
questions.onCorrect: The stack and the redo list are two parts of one history, and a new command ends the redo part.

acceptedIdeas: Clear the redo list when a new command is executed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Clear the redo list when a new command is executed

choices.label: Store each command's old values so that undo can restore them
Clear the redo list when a new command is executed
Remove the oldest command from the stack when the stack is full

misconceptions.feedback: That is what makes undo work, and the undo worked here. The fault lies in what redo may do after a new command.
A full stack is a different problem. The old steps were not too old: they belonged to a history that the new change replaced.

questions.prompt:
A move command is written like this.

`class MoveBy:`
    `def execute(self, p): p.x = max(0, p.x + self.dx)`
    `def undo(self, p): p.x -= self.dx`

A player at x = 3 executes `MoveBy(-5)` and then undoes it. Where does the player end up, and why?
hints: Work out p.x after `execute`, remembering the `max(0, ...)`.
Then apply `undo` to that value and compare the result with where the player started.
questions.onCorrect: A command should save what it changes before it runs, as the old x, and undo should put that value back. The book keeps the previous position in the command for this reason.

acceptedIdeas: At x = 5, since undo reverses the requested move and ignores the actual one
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: At x = 5, since undo reverses the requested move and ignores the actual one

choices.label: At x = 5, since undo reverses the requested move and ignores the actual one
At x = 3, since subtracting the same dx always restores the old position
At x = 0, since the clamp stops undo from moving the player below zero

misconceptions.feedback: The clamp stopped the move at 0, so execute moved the player by only 3, while undo subtracts the full -5. The two do not cancel.
The undo method has no clamp. It computes 0 − (−5), which is 5, so the player ends up beyond the start.

questions.prompt: A team wants its enemies to jump with the same code as the player. How does the command pattern help?
hints: Who creates the command object, and who runs it?
Think about what the key press and the enemy's AI have in common.
questions.onCorrect: A command does not care who issues it, so a key, an AI or a recording can all send the same objects.

acceptedIdeas: The enemy's AI creates the same `Jump` command that a key press creates
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The enemy's AI creates the same `Jump` command that a key press creates

choices.label: Each enemy gets a copy of the player's input handler, so that it can read the keyboard
Every enemy becomes a subclass of the player class, so that jump is inherited
The enemy's AI creates the same `Jump` command that a key press creates

misconceptions.feedback: Enemies do not read the keyboard. The pattern separates whoever issues a request from the code that carries it out.
