Commands are objects apart from the actors that run them, and the command takes the actor as a parameter, so no inheritance is needed.

questions.prompt: Commands A, B, C, D and E are executed. The player undoes twice and then executes F. Which commands are now applied?
hints: Each undo reverses the most recent command that is still applied.
Executing F puts it after the commands that remain, and it clears what could have been redone.
questions.onCorrect: The history is now A, B, C, F, and D and E can no longer be redone.

acceptedIdeas: A, B, C and F
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A, B, C and F

choices.label: A, B, C, D, E and F
A, B and F
A, B, C, D and F
A, B, C and F

misconceptions.feedback: Two undos reversed E and D, and they are not applied again. Executing F then discarded them from the redo list.
Only two commands were undone, E and D. C was never undone, so it is still applied.
That undoes only E. The second undo reversed D as well.

questions.prompt: A game wraps each request as an object, so that it can be stored, queued, replayed or undone. What is the name of this pattern?
hints: The object stands for one action that a game could be asked to carry out.
The same word names the pattern and the objects it makes.
questions.onCorrect: Because a command is an object, it can be kept, passed to another caller and asked to reverse itself.

acceptedIdeas: command
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The command pattern.

misconceptions.feedback: An observer is told when something happens. A command is a request wrapped as an object so that it can be stored and run later.
A memento snapshots an object's whole state. The book finds that wasteful for commands, which change only a small part of it.

questions.prompt: A game has `Flier`, `Swimmer` and `Poisoner` classes, each a subclass of `Monster`. A designer asks for a monster that flies and poisons. What do programmers usually have to do?
hints: The new monster belongs under both `Flier` and `Poisoner`, and a subclass has one parent here.
Think about where the flying code and the poison code would have to live for one class to use both.
questions.onCorrect: Each combination of traits becomes a class of its own, or code is copied between classes. Components avoid both.

acceptedIdeas: Copy the flying or poison code into another class, or invent a parent with no real meaning
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Copy the flying or poison code into another class, or invent a parent with no real meaning

choices.label: Copy the flying or poison code into another class, or invent a parent with no real meaning
Add a class for the new monster and nothing else, since the tree already covers every combination
Nothing, since a class can pick up a new trait while the game runs

misconceptions.feedback: A tree with single parents covers each trait on its own. Each combination of traits needs a class of its own.
A class tree fixes the traits when the code is written. Attaching parts while the game runs is what the component pattern does.

questions.prompt: A game has three independent monster traits, and the team adds a fourth, `breathesFire`. What does that cost in a class tree with a class for every combination, and in a component design?
hints: With four traits, each one on or off, how many combinations can there be?
How many combinations were there with three traits, and how many are new?
questions.onCorrect: Each trait doubles the number of classes, whereas a component design needs only one more part.

acceptedIdeas: Eight new classes in the tree, and one new component in the component design
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Eight new classes in the tree, and one new component in the component design

choices.label: One new class in the tree, since it already holds all of the other combinations
Four new classes in the tree, one for each trait that can join fire
Eight new classes in the tree, and one new component in the component design

misconceptions.feedback: Each of the 8 existing combinations can now also breathe fire, so the tree grows from 8 classes to 16.
Every combination counts, including those with several traits. There are 16 combinations in all, which is 8 more than before.

questions.prompt: In an entity component system, which part holds the code that moves every entity having both a position and a velocity?
hints: Entities are ids and components are data, which leaves one more part.
Which part is described as looping over every entity that has the components it needs?
questions.onCorrect: A system holds the behaviour, so components stay plain data and entities stay bare ids.

acceptedIdeas: A system
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A system

misconceptions.feedback: An entity is only an id, with no data or code of its own.
A component is plain data, such as a position or a velocity, and holds no behaviour.

choices.label: An entity
A component
A system

questions.prompt: A game sums 10,000 positions of 12 bytes each every frame. In one version they sit in a packed array, and in the other each lives inside its own object on the heap. A cache line is 64 bytes. Which version is likely to be faster, and why?
hints: How many 12-byte positions fit in one 64-byte line when they sit side by side?
How many are wanted from each fetch when every position is inside a different object?
questions.onCorrect: A line holds five whole positions, so a packed array needs about one fetch for every five positions, and scattered objects need about one each.

acceptedIdeas: The packed array, since each 64-byte fetch brings in several positions at once
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The packed array, since each 64-byte fetch brings in several positions at once

choices.label: The heap objects, since each fetch brings in a whole object together with its pointers
The packed array, since each 64-byte fetch brings in several positions at once
Neither, since the program does the same arithmetic on the same number of positions

misconceptions.feedback: A fetch brings in 64 bytes of which only 12 are wanted from each object, so the processor waits for memory far more often.
The arithmetic is the same, but the time spent waiting for memory is not. Locality decides how many fetches the loop needs.

questions.prompt: A velocity is 2 floats of 4 bytes each, and 800 velocities are stored in one packed array. How many 64-byte cache lines does the array occupy?
hints: First find the size of one velocity in bytes, then the size of the whole array.
Divide the size of the array by the 64 bytes in a line.
questions.onCorrect: 800 velocities of 8 bytes take 6,400 bytes, which is 100 lines.

acceptedIdeas: 100 lines
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 100 lines

choices.label: 800 lines
100 lines
50 lines

misconceptions.feedback: That gives each velocity a line of its own, which is the worst case for scattered data. Packed velocities share lines, eight to a line.
That counts 4 bytes for each velocity. Each has 2 floats of 4 bytes, which is 8 bytes, so the array takes 6,400 bytes.

questions.prompt: An entity record is 64 bytes: position 12, velocity 12, health 4 and 36 of other data. A collision system, which applies damage on impact, needs position, velocity and health. With 2000 entities, how many 64-byte lines does it read from separate arrays of positions, velocities and health values, packed tightly?
hints: Count the bytes the system actually needs for one entity.
Multiply by the 2000 entities.
Divide the total by 64.
questions.onCorrect: An array of whole 64-byte records would touch 2000 lines, since each record fills a line, so the separate arrays touch a little under half as many.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Position, velocity and health take 12 + 12 + 4 = 28 bytes per entity, so 2000 × 28 = 56 000 bytes, and 56 000 ÷ 64 = 875 lines.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of lines when each 64-byte record is read whole. The question concerns separate arrays.
That is the size in bytes. Divide it by 64 to count lines.
That counts only position and velocity. This system also reads the 4 bytes of health for each entity.

questions.prompt: An invented space game uses an entity component system. Is each of these an entity, a component or a system?
hints: An entity is only an id, a component is plain data and a system is code.
For each item, ask whether it names something, holds data or does work.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ids 7 and 12 are entities, the `Health` array and the `Velocity` record are components, and the movement loop and the removal loop are systems.

items.label: Id 7, which stands for one asteroid
items.explanation: An entity is nothing but an id.

items.label: Id 12, which stands for the player's ship
items.explanation: It is an id that other data is indexed by, and it holds no code.

items.label: The array of `Health` values, one for each entity that has health
items.explanation: It is plain data stored with all the others of its type.

items.label: A `Velocity` record with dx and dy and no behaviour
items.explanation: A component holds data only, and the code that uses it lives elsewhere.

items.label: A loop that adds velocity to position for every entity that has both
items.explanation: The behaviour sits in a system, which loops over the entities that have the components it needs.

items.label: A loop that removes every entity whose health has fallen to 0
items.explanation: It is code that visits entities with a `Health` component, so it is a system.

questions.onCorrect: Keeping data and behaviour apart is what lets one system treat every matching entity the same way.

questions.prompt:
A leader moves 2 units a frame and a follower copies the leader's `x`. They are updated in this order.

`entities = [follower, leader]`
`for frame in range(3):`
    `for e in entities:`
        `e.update()`

After 3 frames the leader is at x = 6 and the follower is at x = 4. Why?
hints: On each frame, which of the two updates first?
When the follower copies `x`, has the leader already moved on that frame?
questions.onCorrect: Updating the leader first gives x = 6 for both. The order in which things update is part of what a game does.

acceptedIdeas: The follower updates before the leader each frame, so it copies where the leader was
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The follower updates before the leader each frame, so it copies where the leader was

choices.label: The follower updates before the leader each frame, so it copies where the leader was
The follower's update is skipped on the first frame, so it starts one whole move behind
The follower can only copy every other value of the leader's `x`, so it falls behind

misconceptions.feedback: Both are updated on every frame. The follower copies on each of them, but it reads the leader's position from the end of the previous frame.
The follower copies on every frame. It stays one move of 2 behind because of the order in which the two update.

questions.prompt: A `Health` component plays the hurt sound by calling `AudioComponent.play('hurt')` directly. A designer asks for a monster with no audio at all. What does this show about the `Health` component?
hints: Which components does an entity need before `Health` can work?
The point of composition is that an entity can hold any mix of parts.
questions.onCorrect: Components that call one another bring back the coupling that composition was meant to remove. The book keeps the domains decoupled so that each part can be used alone.

acceptedIdeas: It depends on another component, so it cannot be used without audio
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It depends on another component, so it cannot be used without audio

choices.label: Nothing is wrong, since a component may call any other component by name
It is too slow, since a call to another component costs a cache miss every time
It depends on another component, so it cannot be used without audio

misconceptions.feedback: Components are meant to stay independent, so that an entity can hold any mix of them. A monster with no `AudioComponent` would crash or need a check everywhere.
Speed is not the trouble here. The fault is the dependence, which stops `Health` being used on an entity that has no audio.

questions.prompt: The damage code tells an achievements listener that the player was hit, and the listener takes 50 ms to run. The game runs at 60 frames per second, so a frame lasts 16.7 ms. What do players see when they take damage?
hints: Does the damage code carry on before the listener has finished?
Divide the listener's time by the length of a frame.
questions.onCorrect: 50 ms is about three frames of 16.7 ms, so the stall is long enough to see.

acceptedIdeas: A hitch of about three frames, since the damage code waits for the listener
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A hitch of about three frames, since the damage code waits for the listener

choices.label: Nothing, since the listener runs once the frame has been drawn and shown
A hitch of about three frames, since the damage code waits for the listener
Only the achievement arrives late, since the listener works in the background thread

misconceptions.feedback: An observer is called at once, and the subject carries on only when it returns. Nothing waits for the end of the frame.
Observers are synchronous. The subject waits for each listener to return, so the whole game stalls.

questions.prompt:
A game keeps a list of listeners for a 'player moved' event.

`for enemy in listeners:`
    `enemy.on_event('player_moved')`

Enemy 2 was destroyed earlier. The log shows `enemy 1 reacts`, then `enemy 2 is dead but still gets player_moved`, then `enemy 3 reacts`. What is the bug?
hints: Read the log: how many times was each enemy called?
Which enemy should no longer be on the list, and who should have taken it off?
questions.onCorrect: A destroyed object that stays registered is called on every event, which wastes time and can crash the game, and the list grows with every one left behind.

acceptedIdeas: The dead enemy was never removed from the list, so it is still called every time
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The dead enemy was never removed from the list, so it is still called every time

choices.label: The event fired three times, so each enemy should have been called only the one time
The listeners are called in the wrong order, so enemy 2 ought to come last of all
The dead enemy was never removed from the list, so it is still called every time

misconceptions.feedback: The event fired once and each listener was called once. The fault is who is still on the list.
Order has nothing to do with it. Enemy 2 should not be on the list at all.

questions.prompt:
A ring buffer of capacity 4 is written like this, with no check for a full buffer.

`buf[tail] = event`
`tail = (tail + 1) % 4`

Five events, e1 to e5, are enqueued before anything is read, and the head is at slot 0. Which event does the next read return?
hints: Follow the tail through five writes: which slots does it use, in order?
Which write lands on a slot that is already holding an event?
questions.onCorrect: A queue that can fill has to decide what to do: refuse the event, overwrite the oldest or grow.

acceptedIdeas: e5, since the fifth write replaced e1 in slot 0
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: e5, since the fifth write replaced e1 in slot 0

choices.label: e5, since the fifth write replaced e1 in slot 0
e1, since a read returns the first event written
e2, since the buffer rejects the fifth event and keeps the first four

misconceptions.feedback: Slot 0 held e1 until the fifth write wrapped round and replaced it, and the head still points at slot 0.
The code has no check for a full buffer, so nothing rejects the write. It overwrites slot 0.

questions.prompt: What does the `% capacity` do in the enqueue line `tail = (tail + 1) % capacity`?
hints: With capacity 4, what would `tail + 1` give after the last slot, slot 3?
Is there a slot at that index in the array?
questions.onCorrect: The remainder after dividing by the capacity brings the index back to 0 after the last slot.

acceptedIdeas: It returns the index to slot 0 after the last slot, so it stays inside the array
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It returns the index to slot 0 after the last slot, so it stays inside the array

choices.label: It lets the buffer hold more events than the number of slots in its array
It returns the index to slot 0 after the last slot, so it stays inside the array
It keeps the head and the tail from ever sitting at the same slot

misconceptions.feedback: The capacity is fixed by the size of the array. The wrap only reuses slots that are already there.
They can meet, when the buffer is empty or full, which is why implementations also keep a count of the events waiting.

questions.prompt: A ring buffer has capacity 6 and its tail index is 4. After 5 enqueues, with `tail = (tail + 1) mod 6` each time, what is the tail index?
hints: Write the tail after each enqueue: 4 becomes 5, then wraps.
Keep going until you have made five enqueues.
questions.onCorrect: The tail runs 5, 0, 1, 2, 3 over the five enqueues.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 5 and never wraps. The index has to stay between 0 and 5, so it returns to 0 after 5.
That stops after four enqueues, which pass through 5, 0, 1 and 2. A fifth enqueue is still to come.

questions.prompt: A player-died event has three synchronous listeners that take 3 ms, 8 ms and 40 ms. At 60 frames per second a frame lasts 16.7 ms. For how many frames' worth of time does the damage code wait, rounded to the nearest whole frame?
hints: The listeners are called one after another, and the damage code waits for every one.
Add the three times, then divide by the length of a frame.
Round the result to the nearest whole frame.
questions.onCorrect: 51 ms is about three frames, so players would see a hitch whenever the event fires.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The damage code waits for all three listeners, 3 + 8 + 40 = 51 ms, and 51 ÷ 16.7 = 3.05, which is 3 frames to the nearest whole frame.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the wait in milliseconds. The question asks for it in frames of 16.7 ms.

questions.prompt: A game uses an event queue for a 'player died' event. In what order do these four things happen?
hints: The sender adds the record and does not wait.
Delivery happens at a chosen point in the game loop, after the sender has moved on.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The damage code posts the record and carries on, the loop later reaches its delivery point, the queue passes the record to each listener, and a listener then does its work.

items: The damage code adds a 'player died' record to the queue and carries on
The game loop reaches the point where it empties the queue
The queue hands the record to each listener
A listener plays the death sound

questions.onCorrect: The sender never waits, and the listeners see the event a little later than it happened.

questions.prompt: To stop the damage code naming every system, a developer makes `AudioSystem`, `UiSystem` and `AchievementSystem` global singletons, so that the damage code calls `AudioSystem.instance.play()` and so on. Why does this not do the job of the observer pattern?
hints: In the observer pattern, does the damage code know which systems are listening?
Count how many systems the damage code names after the change.
questions.onCorrect: The subject should know only that listeners exist, and a global lookup tells it exactly which systems they are.

acceptedIdeas: The damage code still names and calls each system, so a fifth system still means editing it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The damage code still names and calls each system, so a fifth system still means editing it

choices.label: It does, since a global removes the need to pass references, which is all an observer does
The damage code still names and calls each system, so a fifth system still means editing it
It does not, because singletons can only be created once and the damage code needs several of them

misconceptions.feedback: An observer removes the subject's knowledge of who is listening. A global leaves it in place, because the damage code still names every system.
A singleton is created once on purpose, and that is not the trouble. The damage code still has to name and call each system.

questions.prompt: A subject keeps a list of listeners and notifies each of them when something happens, without knowing what they do. What is the name of this pattern?
hints: The listeners watch the subject and are told when it changes.
The name describes the role of the listeners.
questions.onCorrect: The subject knows only that listeners exist, so adding one changes nothing else.

acceptedIdeas: observer
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The observer pattern.

misconceptions.feedback: An event queue holds events until the game chooses to deliver them, so sender and listener are separated in time. The pattern described here notifies directly.
A command wraps a request as an object. Here the subject keeps a list of listeners and tells each one what happened.

questions.prompt: A shooter keeps three bullet slots and reuses them. What is the likeliest cost of having a fixed number of slots?
hints: What happens when a fourth bullet is requested while three slots are in use?
Think about what a fixed number of slots limits.
questions.onCorrect: A fixed number of slots is the point of the idea and also its limit.

acceptedIdeas: A request can arrive when every slot is taken, so the game needs a rule for that case
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A request can arrive when every slot is taken, so the game needs a rule for that case

choices.label: A request can arrive when every slot is taken, so the game needs a rule for that case
Fragmentation comes back after enough bullets have been fired, so memory breaks into gaps
Each bullet takes longer to set up than before, since the pool searches for a slot

misconceptions.feedback: Every slot has the same size and none is ever freed to the system, so no gaps appear between them.
Taking a slot from a free list is quick, which is part of the point of a pool. The cost lies in what happens when no slot is left.

questions.prompt:
A pool of four bullet slots is used like this.

`def spawn(self): return self.free.pop() if self.free else None`
`def on_hit(self, i): self.active.discard(i)`

The player fires six bullets, and each hits something at once. The slots handed out are `[3, 2, 1, 0, None, None]`. What is wrong?
hints: Look at `on_hit`: which list does it change, and which list does `spawn` read?
After four spawns, is there any code that puts a slot back on the free list?
questions.onCorrect: A pool works only if every finished object gives its slot back, and here nothing does.

acceptedIdeas: A bullet that hits is marked inactive, but its slot never returns to the free list
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A bullet that hits is marked inactive, but its slot never returns to the free list

choices.label: Four slots are too few, so the pool should grow whenever it runs out of free slots
A bullet that hits is marked inactive, but its slot never returns to the free list
`pop()` takes the last slot, so it should take the first slot on the free list

misconceptions.feedback: A bigger pool only delays the failure, because no slot ever comes back. Each bullet here is gone in an instant, so even a large pool would drain.
Which end `pop` takes from makes no difference to whether slots come back. None of them is ever returned.

questions.prompt: A designer wants a forest to fit in 1,000,000 bytes. Every tree shares one 20,000-byte mesh and keeps 12 bytes of its own position. What is the largest number of trees that fits?
hints: The mesh is stored once, so take its 20,000 bytes off the budget first.
Divide what is left by the 12 bytes each tree keeps.
Only whole trees count, so round down.
questions.onCorrect: Every tree costs only its own 12 bytes, so the forest can hold more than 80,000 of them, against 49 if each carried a copy of the mesh.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The shared mesh takes 20,000 bytes once, which leaves 980,000 bytes at 12 bytes a tree, and 980,000 ÷ 12 = 81,666.7, so 81,666 whole trees fit.

misconceptions.feedback: That rounds up, and 81,667 trees would need 20,000 + 81,667 × 12 = 1,000,004 bytes, which is 4 over the budget.
That ignores the mesh, 1,000,000 ÷ 12. The shared mesh is paid for once and takes 20,000 bytes of the budget.
That gives every tree its own copy of the mesh, 1,000,000 ÷ 20,012. Sharing is the point of the flyweight.

questions.prompt: In the rock field the mesh is stored once and each rock keeps its own 16 bytes. What decides that the mesh may be shared and the position may not?
hints: Would two rocks ever need different values of the mesh?
Would two rocks ever need different values of position?
questions.onCorrect: The shared part is intrinsic state, which is the same for every instance, and the part that differs is extrinsic state.

acceptedIdeas: Every rock uses the same mesh and never changes it, but each rock sits somewhere else
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Every rock uses the same mesh and never changes it, but each rock sits somewhere else

choices.label: The mesh is the bigger of the two, and large data should always be shared between objects
The position is read more often, and data that is read often belongs to each rock
Every rock uses the same mesh and never changes it, but each rock sits somewhere else

misconceptions.feedback: Size is not the test. Data may be shared when every instance would hold the same value and none changes it.
How often data is read does not decide it. A position differs from rock to rock, so it cannot be shared.

questions.prompt: 2,000 enemies share one 50,000-byte sprite and each keeps 20 bytes of its own state. What is the total memory?
hints: Count the sprite once, since every enemy shares it.
Add the 20 bytes that each of the 2,000 enemies keeps.
questions.onCorrect: 50,000 + 2,000 × 20 = 90,000 bytes, against about 100 million without sharing.

acceptedIdeas: 90,000 bytes
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 90,000 bytes

choices.label: 90,000 bytes
50,020 bytes

misconceptions.feedback: That gives every enemy its own copy of the sprite, 2,000 × 50,020. The flyweight stores the sprite once.
That counts the sprite and the state of one enemy. Each of the 2,000 enemies keeps its own 20 bytes, which is 40,000 bytes.

questions.prompt: A programmer saves 4 bytes per tree by keeping each tree's wind sway inside the shared mesh. What do players see?
hints: How many copies of the sway value exist if it lives in the shared mesh?
Would two trees ever need different values of sway?
questions.onCorrect: Sway differs from tree to tree, so it is extrinsic state and each tree keeps its own.

acceptedIdeas: Every tree sways in step, since all of them read the one shared value
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Every tree sways in step, since all of them read the one shared value

choices.label: Each tree sways on its own, since the mesh is copied when the wind changes
Every tree sways in step, since all of them read the one shared value
The trees stop swaying, since a shared object cannot hold a value that changes

misconceptions.feedback: The mesh is shared, so there is one sway value for all the trees.
It can hold a changing value, and the change shows in every tree at once. Per-instance state belongs outside the flyweight.

questions.prompt: A turn-based card game creates a new `Card` object when a player draws, a handful each minute. Should it use an object pool for them?
hints: How many objects are created and destroyed each second in this game?
A pool trades memory reserved in advance for the absence of allocation. When is that trade worth making?
questions.onCorrect: Both a pool and a flyweight cost something, so each is worth it only when many objects are created and destroyed or when many share large data.

acceptedIdeas: No, since few objects come and go, so a pool's reserved memory would not pay off
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, since few objects come and go, so a pool's reserved memory would not pay off

choices.label: Yes, since a pool makes any game faster, however few objects there are in play
Yes, since cards come in different sizes and would fragment memory over a long game
No, since few objects come and go, so a pool's reserved memory would not pay off

misconceptions.feedback: A pool costs memory reserved in advance, and it pays off only when many objects are created and destroyed during play.
Fragmentation comes from many objects of different sizes being created and freed in no set order, and a handful a minute is far too few.

questions.prompt: A team meets six problems in an invented shooter. Does an object pool or a flyweight fit each one?
hints: A pool helps when many objects are created and destroyed in play.
A flyweight helps when many objects each hold a copy of the same data.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The bullets, the particles and the shell casings suit an object pool, and the bushes, the helmet texture and the lamp posts suit a flyweight.

items.label: Bullets are created and destroyed hundreds of times a second and free memory is breaking into gaps
items.explanation: Objects come and go constantly, which is what a pool of reusable slots is for.

items.label: Frame time spikes whenever an explosion creates sixty particles at once
items.explanation: Particles taken from a pool made at start-up need no allocation in the middle of play.

items.label: Spent shell casings are spawned and freed in a constant stream
items.explanation: A steady stream of short-lived objects is a case for reusing a fixed set of slots.

items.label: Ten thousand bushes each hold their own copy of the same 5,000-byte mesh
items.explanation: The mesh is the same for every bush, so one shared copy will serve them all.

items.label: A thousand soldiers each store the same helmet texture
items.explanation: The texture is identical for every soldier and never changes, so it can be shared.

items.label: Three hundred lamp posts each carry a copy of one model
items.explanation: One model is common to every lamp post, so each post needs only its own position.

questions.onCorrect: A pool saves the cost of creating and freeing objects, and a flyweight saves the memory of copies, so the two solve different problems.

questions.prompt: A shooter has 5 of its 12 memory blocks free, but the longest free run is 2, so an object that needs 3 blocks in a row cannot be placed. What is this problem called?
hints: Enough memory is free in total, but not in one piece.
The name describes memory that has been broken up.
questions.onCorrect: A pool avoids it, because every slot is the same size and none is ever returned to the system.

acceptedIdeas: fragmentation
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Fragmentation, since free memory is broken into small gaps.

misconceptions.feedback: A leak is memory that is never freed. Here the memory is free, and the trouble is that it is scattered in small gaps.
The game is not out of memory, since 5 of 12 blocks are free. No free run is long enough for the object.

questions.prompt: A game tests every entity against every other for collision each frame. An enemy in the far north of a large world is tested against the player in the far south. What does that test tell the game?
hints: Can two entities on opposite sides of the world overlap?
Think about how many of the pairs in a big crowd are like this one.
questions.onCorrect: Most pairs in a large world are far apart, and those tests are wasted.

acceptedIdeas: Almost always nothing, since entities that far apart cannot be touching
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Almost always nothing, since entities that far apart cannot be touching

choices.label: Whether the enemy can see the player, since collision tests also check sight
Almost always nothing, since entities that far apart cannot be touching
Whether the enemy should chase the player, since the test measures distance

misconceptions.feedback: A collision test compares whether two shapes overlap. It says nothing about sight.
The test only reports an overlap, and the enemy's decisions come from other code. A pair this far apart never overlaps.

questions.prompt: A level has 1,000 entities and tests every pair once per frame. The team doubles the crowd to 2,000. How many more pair tests does each frame need, using n(n − 1) ÷ 2?
hints: Find the number of tests for 1,000 entities, then for 2,000, with n(n − 1) ÷ 2.
The question asks for the extra tests, so subtract one count from the other.
The count for 2,000 entities is a little over four times the count for 1,000.
questions.onCorrect: Doubling the crowd makes the work about four times as large, from 499,500 to 1,999,000 tests a frame.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 1,000 entities need 1,000 × 999 ÷ 2 = 499,500 tests and 2,000 entities need 2,000 × 1,999 ÷ 2 = 1,999,000 tests, which is 1,499,500 more.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count for 1,000 entities. The question asks how many more tests the bigger crowd needs.
That is the total for 2,000 entities. Subtract the 499,500 tests the smaller crowd already needed.

questions.prompt:
A grid finds an entity's column like this.

`CELL = 100`
`def column(x): return int(x / CELL)`

An entity at x = -30 and another at x = 30 both get column 0, although the boundary at 0 should separate them. What is wrong?
hints: Work out -30 ÷ 100, and decide which whole number the column should be.
Does `int` round down, or does it drop the fractional part?
questions.onCorrect: The rule is to round down. For positive numbers dropping the fraction does the same, and for negative numbers it does not.

acceptedIdeas: `int` cuts toward zero, so -0.3 becomes 0, and `math.floor` rounds down instead
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `int` cuts toward zero, so -0.3 becomes 0, and `math.floor` rounds down instead

choices.label: `int` cuts toward zero, so -0.3 becomes 0, and `math.floor` rounds down instead
The cell size is too small, so entities near 0 end up sharing a column
Negative coordinates are not allowed in a grid, so the world should start at 0

misconceptions.feedback: A cell 100 units wide keeps -30 and 30 apart once the division rounds down, in columns -1 and 0. The rounding is at fault.
Negative coordinates work when the cell is found by rounding down, which puts -0.3 in column -1.

questions.prompt: An entity is at x = 730 in a world divided into cells 50 units wide, counted from 0. What is its column index?
hints: Divide x by the cell size.
Round the quotient down to a whole number.
questions.onCorrect: 730 ÷ 50 = 14.6, which rounds down to 14.

misconceptions.feedback: That rounds the quotient to the nearest whole number. The column is the one whose range contains 730, so the quotient is rounded down.
That divides by 100. The cells here are 50 units wide, so the quotient is 730 ÷ 50.

questions.prompt: A grid has cells 100 units wide, and the collision test compares each entity only with the others in its own cell. Two 10-unit-wide entities sit at x = 98 and x = 102, close enough to overlap. Their cells are 0 and 1. What happens?
hints: Which cell is each entity filed in?
Which cells would a test have to look at to find a pair that straddles a boundary?
questions.onCorrect: An entity near the edge of its cell can overlap one in the next cell, so the check looks at its own cell and the eight around it.

acceptedIdeas: Their overlap is never tested, since they sit in different cells, so neighbours must be checked
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Their overlap is never tested, since they sit in different cells, so neighbours must be checked

choices.label: They are each tested twice, once from each cell, so the overlap is found with some wasted work in the grid
Their overlap is never tested, since they sit in different cells, so neighbours must be checked
The grid moves one entity into the other's cell when they touch, so the overlap is found

misconceptions.feedback: A test inside a cell compares only the entities that are filed in that cell. Neither entity is filed in the other's cell, so the pair is never compared.
Entities are filed under the cell that holds their position and nothing moves them when they touch. That is why the check has to look at neighbouring cells.

questions.prompt: The entities in a game are about 30 units wide, and the grid cells are 5 units wide. What is the main problem?
hints: Compare the width of an entity with the width of a cell.
Count how many 5-unit cells lie across one 30-unit entity.
questions.onCorrect: Cells much smaller than entities make every entity span several cells, and the bookkeeping outweighs the saving.

acceptedIdeas: Each entity covers many cells and must be filed in every one
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each entity covers many cells and must be filed in every one

choices.label: Every pair of entities is tested twice instead of once
Each entity covers many cells and must be filed in every one
The grid has too few cells to tell the entities apart
Entities can no longer be found from their position

misconceptions.feedback: Counting each pair twice is a separate matter, which is settled by checking pairs in one order.
Tiny cells mean too many cells, not too few. Large cells are the ones that separate little.
The cell index still comes from the position. The difficulty is an entity spanning many cells.

questions.prompt: 1000 entities are spread evenly over 100 cells, so each cell holds 10. Each entity is tested against the others in its own cell and the 8 around it, which together hold 90 entities including itself. Each pair is found from both ends. How many pair tests is that in all?
hints: Remove the entity itself from the 90 in its neighbourhood.
Multiply by the 1000 entities.
Halve the total, since each pair is counted from both ends.
questions.onCorrect: That is about eleven times fewer than the 499,500 tests of the unpartitioned world, and the gap widens as the world grows.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each entity is tested against 90 − 1 = 89 others, so 1000 × 89 = 89,000 tests from the entities' side, and each pair is found twice, so 89,000 ÷ 2 = 44,500.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts each pair twice, once from each end. Halve it.
That is the count for testing every entity against every other, with no grid.
That includes each entity being tested against itself. Remove it, then halve.

questions.prompt: Eight problems from this course each have a pattern that solves them. Which pattern fits each one?
hints: Match each problem to the pattern that was built for it in this course.
Look for the word in each problem that points at a pattern: flags, buttons, memory or distance.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The flag problems suit a state machine, the rebinding and the undo suit commands, the bullets and the particles suit an object pool, and the two collision problems suit a spatial grid.

items.label: A character's flags allow combinations that make no sense, such as jumping and ducking at once
items.explanation: A state variable holds exactly one real state, so impossible combinations cannot arise.

items.label: Each new rule about what may follow what becomes another condition in every place that reads the flags
items.explanation: A transition table holds every state and event pair in one place.

items.label: Players want to rebind the fire button from a settings menu without editing the weapon code
items.explanation: A binding table maps each button to a command object.

items.label: A level editor needs undo and redo
items.explanation: Commands are objects that can be kept and asked to reverse themselves.

items.label: Bullets are created and freed so often that memory breaks into gaps
items.explanation: A pool of same-sized slots is reused, so no gaps appear.

items.label: The frame stalls whenever an explosion creates dozens of particles
items.explanation: Taking particles from a set made at start-up avoids allocation in the middle of play.

items.label: Testing every pair of 5,000 entities for collision takes far too long
items.explanation: Filing entities by position means each is compared only with those nearby.

items.label: Most collision tests compare things on opposite sides of the world
items.explanation: A grid skips pairs in cells that are far apart.

questions.onCorrect: Each pattern removes one kind of trouble and has a cost of its own, so naming the problem comes before picking the pattern.

questions.prompt: A battle puts 900 units in one corner of a huge map, while the rest of the map stays empty. A uniform grid with 100-unit cells puts nearly all of them in a few cells. What fits better?
hints: A uniform grid assumes the entities are spread evenly. Is that true here?
Which structure in the lesson splits only the regions that hold too many entities?
questions.onCorrect: A quadtree divides a square again and again where it is crowded and leaves empty squares alone.

acceptedIdeas: A quadtree, which splits crowded squares into smaller ones and leaves empty areas whole
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A quadtree, which splits crowded squares into smaller ones and leaves empty areas whole

choices.label: A quadtree, which splits crowded squares into smaller ones and leaves empty areas whole
Smaller cells across the whole map, since that spreads the crowd out
Testing every pair, since a crowd this tight cannot be helped by a partition

misconceptions.feedback: That also splits the empty map into huge numbers of useless cells. Only the crowded corner needs splitting, which is what a quadtree does.
900 units need 900 × 899 ÷ 2 = 404,550 tests every frame. A quadtree compares each unit only with those nearby.

questions.prompt: What do we call a structure that splits crowded regions of the world into four smaller squares, again and again, and leaves empty regions whole?
hints: The name refers to the four parts of each split.
It splits a square into four, then splits the crowded squares again.
questions.onCorrect: The cells shrink only where entities are dense, so a crowded corner does not put hundreds of entities in one cell.

acceptedIdeas: quadtree
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: quadtree

questions.prompt: In a game, 200 players start, 150 finish the tutorial, 90 beat level 1 and 45 beat level 2. Which step keeps the smallest share of the players who reach it?
hints: Count the players who reach each step: all 200 reach the tutorial, but only 150 reach level 1.
Compare what each step loses with the number who reached it, not with the 200 who started.
questions.onCorrect: Level 2 keeps 45 of the 90 players who reach it, half, against three fifths at level 1 and three quarters at the tutorial.

acceptedIdeas: Level 2
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Level 2

choices.label: The tutorial
Level 1
Level 2

misconceptions.feedback: The tutorial loses 50 of the 200 players who reach it, a quarter, so it keeps three quarters, the largest share of the three steps.
Level 1 loses the most players, 60, but it was reached by 150. It keeps 90 of them, three fifths, a larger share than the final step keeps of its 90.

questions.prompt: In a card game, which of these statements describes a mechanic?
hints: A mechanic is a rule or a piece of data that a program could check.
Ask whether each statement is a rule, a habit of play or a feeling.

acceptedIdeas: Each player draws five cards at the start of a round.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each player draws five cards at the start of a round.

questions.onCorrect: It is a rule with a number in it, which a program can check at the start of every round.

choices.label: Each player draws five cards at the start of a round.
Players keep their best card until the final round.
The suspense of waiting for the last card.

misconceptions.feedback: Holding a card back is behaviour that appears when people play, which makes it a dynamic. No rule asks players to do it.
Suspense is a feeling the player has, so it is an aesthetic. A rule can make the feeling more likely but cannot state it.

questions.prompt: A shooter quietly gives the player extra health after each death and never says so. Players eventually find out. What is the main risk of this adaptive approach?
hints: Think about what a player who finds out would conclude about a win.
A player who loses should be able to say why. What could this player say?

acceptedIdeas: Players may feel that their wins were not earned
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Players may feel that their wins were not earned

questions.onCorrect: A player who finds the adjustment stops believing that a win was earned, even when the measuring is accurate.

choices.label: Players can no longer choose a difficulty level
The difficulty curve turns into a straight ramp
The game can no longer count how often players die
Players may feel that their wins were not earned

misconceptions.feedback: Selectable difficulty is a separate approach, and quiet adjustment does not remove it by itself.
The adjustment moves the challenge up and down, so the curve stays uneven. The risk comes from what players make of it.
The game still counts deaths, since the extra health depends on that count. The trouble lies in how players read the result.

questions.prompt: Why is the health divided by 112.5, the damage per second, and not by 75, the damage per hit?
hints: Think about the unit of each answer: what does health divided by each of the two numbers measure?
Health is a count of points and the rate is points per second. Which division leaves seconds?

acceptedIdeas: Dividing by a rate leaves seconds, but dividing by damage per hit leaves hits
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Dividing by a rate leaves seconds, but dividing by damage per hit leaves hits

questions.onCorrect: Health divided by damage per second leaves seconds, and health divided by damage per hit would leave hits, which is why only the first gives a time to kill.

choices.label: The damage per hit leaves out the critical hits that the weapon also deals
Each hit takes one second, so dividing by damage per hit would also give seconds
Dividing by a rate leaves seconds, but dividing by damage per hit leaves hits

misconceptions.feedback: The 75 is already the expected damage per hit, so it includes the critical hits. The two divisions differ in what they leave in the answer.
This weapon lands 1.5 hits in every second, so a count of hits is not a count of seconds.

questions.prompt: A team wants to learn whether players understand the jump in a tutorial. Which question can a playtest answer?
hints: A testable question can be answered by watching what a player does.
Which question names something that a player does or does not do?
questions.onCorrect: The question names something that a player either does or does not do, so watching can settle it.

acceptedIdeas: How many players clear the first gap on the first try?
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: How many players clear the first gap on the first try?

choices.label: Is the jump tutorial well designed for the people who will play it?
Can every kind of player learn to jump from this one tutorial?
Do players enjoy the tutorial level more than the one before it?
How many players clear the first gap on the first try?

misconceptions.feedback: Well designed has no observable meaning until it is turned into something a player does.
Every kind of player is far too wide for one session, and no observation settles it.
Enjoyment is an opinion, and players are polite. Watching what they do is stronger evidence.

questions.prompt: 300 players started, 240 finished the tutorial and 168 beat level 1. What percentage of the players who reached level 1 beat it?
hints: Which group of players reached level 1?
Divide the players who beat level 1 by that group.
questions.onCorrect: 168 of the 240 who reached level 1 beat it, which is 70 percent.

acceptedIdeas: 70 percent
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 70 percent

choices.label: 56 percent
30 percent
70 percent

misconceptions.feedback: That divides 168 by the 300 who started the game. The share for a step is taken out of the players who reached that step, which is 240.
That is the share who left at level 1, 72 of the 240. The question asks for the share who beat it.

questions.prompt: A ball moves at 900 pixels per second and a wall is 10 pixels thick. A heavy scene drops the game to 20 updates per second, and now the ball sometimes passes through the wall with no collision. What happens?
hints: Divide the speed by the number of updates per second to find the distance moved per update.
Compare that distance with the thickness of the wall.
questions.onCorrect: A step longer than the wall can put the ball on one side and then on the other without any update in which they overlap.

acceptedIdeas: Each update moves the ball 45 pixels, more than the wall's thickness, so it can skip over
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each update moves the ball 45 pixels, more than the wall's thickness, so it can skip over

choices.label: Each update moves the ball 45 pixels, more than the wall's thickness, so it can skip over
The wall's collision box shrinks whenever the frame rate falls, so the ball finds it harder to hit
Delta time is zero on slow frames, so the ball never gets as far as the wall's position

misconceptions.feedback: A wall does not change with the frame rate. The ball's step does, and at 20 updates a second each step is 45 pixels long.
On a slow frame the delta time is larger. A larger delta time makes each step bigger, and a big step can jump over a thin wall.

questions.prompt: A ducking state shrinks the character's hitbox when the machine moves into it. Which of the state's methods should put the hitbox back to full size when the machine leaves?
hints: The hitbox has to change back once, at one particular moment in the state's life.
Setup runs once on the way into a state. What runs once on the way out?

acceptedIdeas: `exit`
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `exit`

questions.onCorrect: The change is made once, on the way out, so `update` stays free for the work that repeats every frame.

choices.label: `enter`
`update`
`exit`

misconceptions.feedback: `enter` runs once as the machine moves into the state, which is where the hitbox was shrunk. The machine has not left yet.
`update` runs on every tick while the machine stays in the state. Restoring the hitbox there would undo the shrinking while the character is still ducking.

questions.prompt: A machine has three states: idle, jumping and ducking. Jump takes idle to jumping, duck takes idle to ducking, and land takes jumping to idle. Every other pair of state and event has no entry. Starting in idle, the machine receives the events jump, duck, land, jump. Which state is it in at the end?
hints: Follow the events one at a time, and look for any pair of state and event that has no entry.
A pair of state and event with no entry leaves the state unchanged.

acceptedIdeas: Jumping
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Jumping

questions.onCorrect: Duck found no entry while the machine was jumping, so it changed nothing, and the last jump then started from idle.

choices.label: Jumping
Idle
Ducking

misconceptions.feedback: That is the state after land. One more event follows it.
Duck takes idle to ducking, but the machine had already left idle when duck arrived, and the state it was in then has no entry for it.

questions.prompt: A game lets players choose which button fires the weapon from a settings menu. Which design allows this without editing the code that fires the weapon?
hints: Which design puts the button in data and not in code?
The binding table of the lesson sits between the keys and the actions.

acceptedIdeas: A table that maps each button to a command object
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A table that maps each button to a command object

questions.onCorrect: The table holds the button, the command does the work, and only the table changes when a button is rebound.

choices.label: A longer chain of if statements, one per button
A table that maps each button to a command object
A global flag that records the last button pressed
A separate copy of the firing code for each button

misconceptions.feedback: Each new button adds another branch to the chain, so the game logic changes whenever a button does.
A flag records a fact about the game and does not say which button does what.
Each copy stays tied to its own button in the code, so changing a button still means editing code.

questions.prompt: Why can C no longer be redone once D has been executed?
hints: Redo applies a command after the one that was applied last.
Ask what history C would be added to if it were redone after D.

acceptedIdeas: Redoing it would put it after D, in a history that never contained it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Redoing it would put it after D, in a history that never contained it

questions.onCorrect: The redo branch describes a future that no longer follows from the new history, so it is cleared.

choices.label: A command can be redone only once after it has been undone
The stack holds at most three commands, and D took the last place
Redoing it would put it after D, in a history that never contained it

misconceptions.feedback: C has not been redone at all yet, so a limit on repeated redos is not what stops it.
The stack has no fixed size. After D it holds A, B and D, and it could hold many more.

questions.prompt: Commands A, B, C, D, E and F are executed. The player undoes 3 times, executes G, then undoes once. How many commands can be redone now?
hints: Write down which commands are applied and which are waiting to be redone after each step.
What happens to the redo list the moment G is executed?
questions.onCorrect: After G the history is A, B, C, G. Undoing once leaves A, B and C applied with G waiting.

acceptedIdeas: 1 command
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 1 command

choices.label: 4 commands
3 commands
1 command

misconceptions.feedback: That adds G to D, E and F. Executing G ended the redo branch, so D, E and F were discarded and only G can be redone.
That counts D, E and F, the commands undone before G. Executing G discarded them.

questions.prompt: The packed array fills 120 lines, but a line of its own for each position would take 640. Why does packing the positions together need so many fewer lines?
hints: Think about how many 12-byte positions fit in a 64-byte line.
Compare 640 lines with 120 and ask how many positions share one line.

acceptedIdeas: Each line holds several 12-byte positions, so one fetch brings in many of them
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each line holds several 12-byte positions, so one fetch brings in many of them

questions.onCorrect: A line holds five 12-byte positions, so one fetch serves five of them and the array needs about a fifth of the lines.

choices.label: Each line holds several 12-byte positions, so one fetch brings in many of them
Packed positions are stored in fewer bytes than scattered ones
The processor skips the bytes in a line that the program does not need

misconceptions.feedback: A position takes 12 bytes however it is stored. What changes is how many positions share a line.
The processor fetches the whole line, whether the program wants all of it or not.

questions.prompt: A listener only updates the health number on screen. It takes under 1 ms, and the number must show the new value in the same frame as the hit. Which design fits better?
hints: Compare what the listener costs with how soon its work must be done.
The number must show in the same frame as the hit. Which design can promise that?

acceptedIdeas: A synchronous observer
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A synchronous observer

questions.onCorrect: The listener is quick and its work must appear in the same frame, so waiting for it costs almost nothing, and the observer delivers the event at once.

choices.label: An event queue delivered at the start of the next update
A synchronous observer
Direct calls from the damage code to the interface

misconceptions.feedback: A queue delivers the event a little later than it happened, and here the number must change in the same frame. The listener is also quick enough that waiting for it costs almost nothing.
Direct calls would work, but they make the damage code depend on the interface, which is the coupling an observer removes.

questions.prompt: A game has thousands of enemies of three kinds. Which of these belongs in the flyweight for one kind, the data shared by every enemy of that kind?
hints: Shared data must be identical for every enemy of the kind, and no enemy may change it.
For each option, ask whether two enemies of the same kind would ever differ.

acceptedIdeas: The top speed set for its kind
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The top speed set for its kind

questions.onCorrect: The speed set for the kind is the same for every enemy of it and no enemy changes it, so one copy can serve them all.

choices.label: Its position
Its current health
The target it is chasing now
The top speed set for its kind

misconceptions.feedback: Each enemy stands somewhere different, so its position is extrinsic and stored for each enemy.
Health falls as each enemy is hurt, so it differs from one enemy to the next and has to be kept with each.
Each enemy may chase something different, and the target changes over time, so it stays with the enemy.

questions.prompt: Why is the quotient 4.8 rounded down to column 4 and not up to column 5?
hints: Work out which range of x values column 4 covers.
A column holds every x from its left edge up to the start of the next column.

acceptedIdeas: Column 4 covers x from 400 up to 500, so the entity at 480 is inside it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Column 4 covers x from 400 up to 500, so the entity at 480 is inside it

questions.onCorrect: Rounding down makes every position within a cell give the same index, so each cell owns exactly the positions from its starting edge up to the next one.

choices.label: Column 4 covers x from 400 up to 500, so the entity at 480 is inside it
The entity is closer to the start of column 4 than to the start of column 5
Ordinary rounding of 4.8 gives 4 as well, so nothing special is needed

misconceptions.feedback: At x = 480 the entity is 80 units from the start of column 4 and 20 from the start of column 5. Nearness to an edge does not decide the cell.
Ordinary rounding of 4.8 gives 5. Grid indexes round down for a reason of their own.

flashcards.front: In MDA, what are the emotional responses a player has called?
flashcards.back: They are the aesthetics, and a designer can only reach them by way of the mechanics and dynamics.

acceptedIdeas: aesthetics
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: aesthetics

flashcards.front: What do we call the longer cycles, such as unlocks, that give the core loop a reason to repeat?
flashcards.back: Outer loops wrap the core loop and change what the next pass is like.

acceptedIdeas: outer loops
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: outer loops

flashcards.front: Why is a list of features not a loop?
flashcards.back: A loop has an order and returns the player to the first action with the state changed, which a list does not say.

flashcards.front: At 60 frames per second, how long is one frame in ms, to one decimal place?
flashcards.back: A second holds 60 frames, so a frame lasts 1000 ÷ 60 = 16.7 ms.

flashcards.front: What is the delay between an input and its visible response called?
flashcards.back: Latency, which a designer counts in frames so that it does not depend on the machine.

acceptedIdeas: latency
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: latency

flashcards.front: Why can a control feel responsive even when its full motion takes a long time?
flashcards.back: The response begins on the very next frame, so the player sees at once that the input was received.

flashcards.front: What is the state of absorption called that arises when challenge matches skill and the goals and feedback are clear?
flashcards.back: Csikszentmihalyi called it flow, and it sits between boredom and anxiety.

acceptedIdeas: flow
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: flow

flashcards.front: Why can the same level bore a player who has improved?
flashcards.back: Skill rose while the challenge stayed fixed, which moves the player below the flow channel.

flashcards.front: What is it called when a racing game speeds up the trailing cars to keep the race close?
flashcards.back: It is called rubber-banding, and players who notice it can feel the result is unfair.

acceptedIdeas: rubber-banding
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: rubber-banding

flashcards.front: A hit does 50 damage and 10% of hits crit for triple damage. What is the expected damage per hit?
flashcards.back: 0.9 × 50 + 0.1 × 150 = 60, because each outcome is weighted by how often it happens.

flashcards.front: Time to kill is health divided by what?
flashcards.back: Health divided by damage per second gives the seconds a fight lasts.

acceptedIdeas: damage per second
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: damage per second

flashcards.front: Why can a formula find an outlier but not tell you whether a game is fun?
flashcards.back: A formula measures numbers such as damage or cost, while fun is a feeling that only play can show.

flashcards.front: What is a cheap, quick version of a game built to answer one design question called?
flashcards.back: A prototype answers one question, so it needs only enough to answer it.

acceptedIdeas: prototype
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: prototype

flashcards.front: 100 players reach level 3 and 60 of them beat it. What percentage of those who reached it beat it?
flashcards.back: 60 ÷ 100 is 60 percent, measured against those who reached the step.

flashcards.front: Why is a designer's own play not a playtest?
flashcards.back: The designer already knows the rules and where everything is, so cannot show where a new player would hesitate.

flashcards.front: What name is given to the unspent real time that a fixed-timestep loop carries from one frame to the next?
flashcards.back: The accumulator holds it, and each update spends one step from it.

acceptedIdeas: accumulator
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: accumulator

flashcards.front: The step is 25 ms. Frames take 60, 30 and 40 ms in turn, with lag starting at 0. How many updates run in total?
flashcards.back: The frames give 2, 1 and 2 updates, leaving 5 ms at the end.

flashcards.front: Why is the loop not simply 'running at 60 frames per second'?
flashcards.back: The update rate is fixed by the step while the render rate follows the machine, and the accumulator joins the two.

flashcards.front: A character has `isJumping`, `isDucking` and `isDiving` flags. Why can its code reach states that make no sense?
flashcards.back: Nothing stops two flags from being true together, and three flags allow eight combinations of which only four are real. A state variable names only the real states.

flashcards.front: A single variable that holds exactly one of a fixed set of values, replacing a pile of flags, is called what kind of variable?
flashcards.back: One state variable can only hold a real state, so no impossible combination exists.

acceptedIdeas: state
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: state

flashcards.front: Why is a state machine not only for enemy AI?
flashcards.back: Player control, menus and animation all have a fixed set of states with rules for moving between them.

flashcards.front: A table that maps inputs to commands, so keys can be rebound without editing game logic, is called an input what?
flashcards.back: A binding table keeps keys in data, so changing a key changes a row and not the code.

acceptedIdeas: binding
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: binding

flashcards.front: Commands A, B and C are executed and the player undoes once. How many commands are applied?
flashcards.back: The undo reverses C, so A and B remain applied.

flashcards.front: Why does undo not need to save the whole game state after each command?
flashcards.back: A command can store only what it needs to reverse itself, such as an object's old position.

flashcards.front: A position is 3 floats of 4 bytes. How many whole positions fit in one 64-byte cache line?
flashcards.back: Each position takes 12 bytes, and 64 ÷ 12 gives 5 whole positions.

flashcards.front: What is the name for the unit of memory, commonly 64 bytes, that a processor fetches at a time?
flashcards.back: A whole cache line is fetched even when only part of it is wanted.

acceptedIdeas: cache line
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: cache line

flashcards.front: Why is ECS not always faster than ordinary objects?
flashcards.back: Locality helps only when many entities share the same components, and the pattern costs extra complexity elsewhere.

flashcards.front: What is the name of a fixed array whose write index wraps to zero after reaching the end?
flashcards.back: This is a ring buffer: the wrapping index makes a fixed array behave as a ring, so no memory is moved.

acceptedIdeas: ring buffer
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: ring buffer

flashcards.front: A ring buffer has capacity 4 and tail 3. After one enqueue, what is the tail?
flashcards.back: (3 + 1) mod 4 = 0, so the index wraps to the first slot.

flashcards.front: Why can a slow listener hurt a synchronous observer but not a queue?
flashcards.back: A synchronous subject waits for each listener to finish, while a queue lets it hand the event over and carry on.

flashcards.front: What is the pattern called that keeps one copy of shared, unchanging data and lets many instances refer to it?
flashcards.back: In the flyweight pattern the shared data is stored once, and each instance keeps only its own extrinsic state.

acceptedIdeas: flyweight
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: flyweight

flashcards.front: A bullet pool hands out its four slots, but after four shots no more bullets appear even though the bullets are gone. What is the likeliest fault?
flashcards.back: A bullet that ends is marked inactive but its slot is never put back on the free list, so the pool drains and stays empty.

flashcards.front: Why is a pool not always a win?
flashcards.back: It reserves memory up front, even when little is used, and the game must decide what to do when every slot is taken.

flashcards.front: How many pairwise tests do 100 entities need, using n(n − 1) ÷ 2?
flashcards.back: 100 × 99 ÷ 2 = 4,950, because each pair needs only one test.

flashcards.front: Dividing the world into equal cells and storing each entity in the cell that holds its position is called a ___ grid.
flashcards.back: In a uniform grid the equal cells make the cell index a simple division of the position.

acceptedIdeas: uniform
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: uniform

flashcards.front: Why check the neighbouring cells as well as an entity's own cell?
flashcards.back: Entities near a cell's edge can touch entities that are stored in the adjacent cell.

sources.title: MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research (Hunicke, LeBlanc, Zubek, 2004)
sources.publisher: Hunicke, LeBlanc and Zubek (hosted at Northwestern University)
sources.licence: Workshop paper, © authors; freely available
sources.notes: Defines mechanics, dynamics and aesthetics, gives the designer's and the player's direction of reading, and lists the eight kinds of aesthetic.

sources.title: Game Design Concepts, Level 5: Mechanics and Dynamics (Ian Schreiber, 2009)
sources.licence: CC BY 3.0 US (stated on the blog's front page)
sources.section: Level 5, the sections on the MDA framework and on positive and negative feedback loops
sources.notes: Explains mechanics, dynamics and aesthetics with examples, and describes the negative feedback loop in kart racing games that helps trailing players catch up.

sources.title: Loops and Arcs (Daniel Cook, Lostgarden, 2012)
sources.licence: Copyright Daniel Cook; free to read online
sources.notes: Describes a game loop as action, rules, feedback and an updated mental model that starts the loop again, and says loops are nested at several levels and frequencies. The article does not use the terms core loop and outer loop.

sources.title: Game Feel: The Secret Ingredient (Steve Swink, Game Developer, 2007)
sources.licence: Copyright Informa; free to read online
sources.section: The six pieces of game feel: input, response, context, polish, metaphor and rules
sources.notes: The article behind Swink's later book. Supports the definition of game feel, its parts, and polish effects such as screen shake.

sources.title: Programming Responsiveness (Mick West, Game Developer, 2008)
sources.licence: Copyright Informa; free to read online
sources.section: The discussion of response lag around Figure 1
sources.notes: Counts the delay between a button press and visible feedback in frames, and shows that the same number of frames is twice the time at 30 frames per second as at 60.

sources.title: Celeste & Forgiveness (Maddy Thorson, Maddy Makes Games)
sources.licence: Copyright Maddy Thorson; free to read online
sources.notes: Names coyote time: the player can still jump for a short time after leaving a ledge.

sources.title: The Role of Animations in Hit Effects (Peyman Massoudi, Game Developer, 2016)
sources.licence: Copyright Informa; free to read online
sources.section: The sections on camera shakes and "Hit Pauses"
sources.notes: Describes hit pauses, where time stops briefly when an attack lands, and camera shake as feedback for a hit.

sources.title: Game Design Concepts, Level 7: Decision-Making and Flow Theory (Ian Schreiber, 2009)
sources.licence: CC BY 3.0 US (stated on the blog's front page)
sources.section: Level 7, sections "Flow theory", "Flow States in Games" and "One Slight Problem"
sources.notes: Covers Csikszentmihalyi's flow, boredom when skill outruns challenge, and the answers to it: rising difficulty, difficulty levels and dynamic difficulty adjustment.

sources.title: Flow in Games (and Everything Else) (Jenova Chen, Communications of the ACM 50(4), 2007)
sources.publisher: Association for Computing Machinery (copy on the author's site)
sources.licence: © 2007 ACM; free to read on the author's site
sources.section: Pages 31 to 33, including the diagram of the flow zone between anxiety and boredom
sources.notes: Dates the concept of flow to the mid-1970s, cites the 1990 book, and describes anxiety above the flow zone and boredom below it.

sources.title: Game Balance Concepts, Level 4: Probability and Randomness (Ian Schreiber, 2010)
sources.licence: CC BY 3.0 US (stated on the blog's front page)
sources.section: Level 4, the parts on expected value
sources.notes: Computes an expected value by multiplying each result by its probability and adding the products.

sources.title: Game Balance Concepts, Level 2: Numeric Relationships (Ian Schreiber, 2010)
sources.licence: CC BY 3.0 US (stated on the blog's front page)
sources.section: Level 2, sections "Identity and Linear Relationships" and "Exponential and Triangular Relationships"
sources.notes: Sets out linear and exponential relationships between a game's numbers, which the growth curves use.

sources.title: Game Balance Concepts, Level 10: Final Boss (Ian Schreiber, 2010)
sources.licence: CC BY 3.0 US (stated on the blog's front page)
sources.section: Level 10, "Economic Systems", subsections "Open and closed economies" and "Inflation"
sources.notes: Explains inflation in a game economy where money keeps entering, and money sinks that remove it.

sources.title: Game Design Concepts, Level 4: The Early Stages of the Design Process (Ian Schreiber, 2009)
sources.licence: CC BY 3.0 US (stated on the blog's front page)
sources.notes: Says a prototype exists to make iteration fast and that paper is the cheap way to build one.

sources.title: Game Design Concepts, Level 14: Playing with Non-Designers (Ian Schreiber, 2009)
sources.licence: CC BY 3.0 US (stated on the blog's front page)
sources.section: Level 14, the advice on observing testers
sources.notes: Tells the designer to watch testers and take notes instead of asking whether the game is fun, and not to step in when they get stuck.

sources.title: Game Balance Concepts, Level 8: Metrics and Statistics (Ian Schreiber, 2010)
sources.licence: CC BY 3.0 US (stated on the blog's front page)
sources.notes: Covers measuring what players do in a game and reading the numbers with care. It does not use the words telemetry or funnel.

sources.title: Game Programming Patterns: Game Loop (Robert Nystrom, 2014)
sources.licence: © 2009-2021 Robert Nystrom; free to read online
sources.notes: Variable and fixed time steps, the lag variable and the update loop that spends it in whole steps.

sources.title: Fix Your Timestep! (Glenn Fiedler, Gaffer On Games, 2004)
sources.licence: © Glenn Fiedler; free to read

sources.title: Game Programming Patterns: State (Robert Nystrom, 2014)
sources.licence: © 2009-2021 Robert Nystrom; free to read online
sources.notes: Boolean flags against a finite state machine, the state pattern with enter and exit actions, and hierarchical state machines.

sources.title: Game Programming Patterns: Command (Robert Nystrom, 2014)
sources.licence: © 2009-2021 Robert Nystrom; free to read online
sources.notes: Configurable input, commands that take an actor, AI that emits commands, replay, and undo and redo with a list of commands.

sources.title: Game Programming Patterns: Component (Robert Nystrom, 2014)
sources.licence: © 2009-2021 Robert Nystrom; free to read online
sources.notes: Why inheritance fails when traits combine, building an object from components, and the note on entity component systems where an entity is only an ID.

sources.title: Game Programming Patterns: Data Locality (Robert Nystrom, 2014)
sources.licence: © 2009-2021 Robert Nystrom; free to read online
sources.notes: Cache lines, cache misses, packing components into contiguous arrays, and hot/cold splitting.

sources.title: Game Programming Patterns: Observer (Robert Nystrom, 2014)
sources.licence: © 2009-2021 Robert Nystrom; free to read online
sources.notes: The achievements example, synchronous notification where a slow observer blocks the subject, and the lapsed listener problem.

sources.title: Game Programming Patterns: Event Queue (Robert Nystrom, 2014)
sources.licence: © 2009-2021 Robert Nystrom; free to read online
sources.notes: Queued events decouple sender and receiver in time, and the ring buffer with head and tail indices that wrap with modulo.

sources.title: Game Programming Patterns: Object Pool (Robert Nystrom, 2014)
sources.licence: © 2009-2021 Robert Nystrom; free to read online
sources.notes: Memory fragmentation, a fixed pool of reusable objects, the free list, and what to do when the pool is full.

sources.title: Game Programming Patterns: Flyweight (Robert Nystrom, 2014)
sources.licence: © 2009-2021 Robert Nystrom; free to read online
sources.notes: The forest of trees that share one mesh, and intrinsic against extrinsic state.

sources.title: Game Programming Patterns: Spatial Partition (Robert Nystrom, 2014)
sources.licence: © 2009-2021 Robert Nystrom; free to read online
sources.notes: Pairwise tests that grow with the square of the number of units, the fixed grid with cell indices and neighbouring cells, and quadtrees.
